items.title: Peoples' iron comes only from banded iron formations, so pre-industrial iron is confined to exposed cratons at least 1.8 Gyr old
items.evidence: planet/lineages/land.py:72 maps the good "iron" to ("bif_fe",) and nothing else. planet/resources.py:594 sets bif_fe = craton * ramp(age, 1800, 2700) * exposed * ...; the model text at resources.py:49-50 reads 'ancient (>= 1.8 Gyr) shield crust'. Searching planet/ for bog iron, limonite, siderite, ironstone or ferricrete finds nothing. Wetlands and bogs already exist as data: vegetation.py:419 'raised bog', gameattrs.py:234 'bog', and soils have PEAT. World 067778 shows iron (bif_fe) on 2.44% of land, all of it on old shields.
items.why_it_matters: Before the 19th-20th century almost all iron came from bog ore, limonite/goethite (lateritic ferricrete), siderite clay-ironstones in coal measures, oolitic ironstones (Minette, Cleveland), magnetite sands and skarns. BIF/taconite and BIF-derived hematite were barely worked before industrial beneficiation. For a culinary ethnography (iron pots, griddles, knives, ploughshares) this decides which peoples have iron at all. Today any people without an old shield is iron-poor, and that is a lie the lineage notes then repeat (showcase-4: '15 of the world's 389 iron districts').
items.recommendation: Add pre-industrial iron deposit models from layers that already exist. Bog iron: wetland/peat cells over a cool-temperate or boreal climate. Lateritic ferricrete: the same tropical-weathering streaks as bauxite, on mafic rock and also on non-mafic rock. Siderite and oolitic ironstone: shale or coal strata near the surface. Black-sand placers: below arc and hotspot basalt. Map 'iron' in land.py to the max of these and bif_fe, and keep BIF as the 'high-grade, needs industry' iron. A small data-only change in resources.py and land.py, with no run changes.
items.verify_reason: Checked. planet/lineages/land.py:72 maps iron to ("bif_fe",) and nothing else. resources.py:49-50 and :594 put BIF on cratons >=1.8 Gyr. No bog-iron, ironstone, siderite or ferricrete model exists anywhere in planet/. The real-world claim is right: before industrial beneficiation, iron came mostly from bog ore, limonite/laterite, clay-ironstones, oolitic ironstones and skarns, not from taconite BIF. The fix is data-only and cheap, but it decides which peoples have iron, which is central to the culinary goal. Peoples are a light v0 pass, not the v1 physics bar, so it stays high but is not a blocker.

items.title: Continental shelves are 2-8x scarcer than on the Earth world at the same grid; submerged continent sits at slope depths (-0.7 to -1.6 km median, against Earth's -184 m)
items.evidence: Read-only on stored worlds. Share of ocean cells between -200 and 0 m: Earth world 506694 (L6, ETOPO) 5.8%. Model worlds near zero sea-level change: 6909cb 1.4%, 6fbc2c 0.7%, e71172 0.9%, 81aced 0.6%, 2a7385 0.6%, 607540 0.6%, 3e9e7d 5.1%, d14b89 3.2% (glacial-lowstand worlds 067778/1df1c3 are ~0.4%). Median depth of submerged continental crust: Earth -184 m; model -680 to -1593 m (6909cb -1210, 6fbc2c -1506, e71172 -1481, 81aced -1593). Ice-free land below 200 m: Earth 26%, model 8-34% (median ~17%). Mechanism candidates: surface.py:170-194, where only cells above SHELF_EDGE (-400 m) fill to SHELF_TOP and deeper margin cells keep only 1-exp(-d/fan_km) (~5-10% per cell), so shelves can hardly prograde; rifted-margin crust of 12-18 km (crust.py, rift_margin_km) stands at -2.3..-3.2 km; and isostasy.elevation (isostasy.py:221) uses the air-loaded 150 m/km for continental crust below sea level, where water loading gives ~220 m/km. That last error makes margins too shallow, so it isn't the cause, but it is a physics inconsistency. Neither tools/scorecard.py nor earth_check measures shelf area or hypsometry, and no ticket tracks it.
items.why_it_matters: Shelves (~7.5% of Earth's ocean) carry most of the world's fisheries, shellfish beds, tidal flats, seagrass, sea-salt pans, carbonate platforms and the epeiric-sea source rocks for oil. The culinary goal's fishing and salt goods (PW-732: 'fisheries (shelf seas...)') rest on them. The shortfall is probably also behind PW-130 (karst 0.3-0.4% of land against Earth ~10%), because carbonate platforms need wide shallow shelves, and the low lowland share means fewer coastal plains and floodplain farmland.
items.recommendation: Add a hypsometry check (ocean share 0..-200 m, land share <200 m, median depth of submerged continent) to scorecard against the Earth world at the same level. Then test the cheapest mechanism: let sediment reaching margin cells below SHELF_EDGE fill toward the shelf's level next to the shelf (clinoform progradation), rather than fanning 63% of it over 1000 km of abyss. Also fix the water-loaded isostasy for submerged continental crust. Put this on the run-physics lane before the v1 showcase remake, because it changes coasts for every downstream system.

items.title: The CO2 weathering sink is all physical erosion of any rock with no kinetic ceiling, and decisions.md records a 'saturating law' ruling the code never got
items.evidence: earth.py:97-110: supply = sim.weathered * land, and sim.weathered = sim.removed (earth.py:711), the total mass eroded from the cell, cover and basement alike. It has no lithology factor, so eroded limestone (CO2-neutral on long timescales), evaporite (no CO2; erodibility 3.0, surface.py, the fastest-eroding rock) and coal/kerogen (a CO2 source when oxidised) all count as silicate drawdown, and basalt (5-10x the weatherability of granite, Dessert et al. 2003) counts the same as quartz sandstone. docs/wiki/decisions.md:33 says '2026-10-22 · Weathering · smooth saturating law, no hard cutoff · PW-574', but PW-574's Updates say attempt 1 failed and the ticket was 'Superseded by PW-576 option C'. grep finds no saturation in earth.py or surface.py. PW-708's diagnosis is that the late cooling is 'weatherability: the weathering supply is ~12-20% higher late' (relief), and the star's 0.45 was brought in to cancel that trend (star-anchor audit #3).
items.why_it_matters: The chain 'erosion rises late → sink rises → cooling → star 0.45 picked to cancel it' rests on a supply-limited, lithology-blind sink. Real chemical weathering saturates at high erosion rates (West et al. 2005; Maher & Chamberlain 2014) and depends strongly on lithology. Salt basins and limestone uplands drawing down CO2 like basalt is a quiet error under a calibrated star. The ruling log also tells a coordinator something exists that doesn't.
items.recommendation: Correct decisions.md:33 now: mark it superseded by PW-576 C and say the sink is unsaturated. Open a needs-decision ticket on the run-physics lane, after the star anchor work (PW-813/815): weight supply by the silicate share of what eroded (x[:, MIX] already tracks carbonate, evaporite, coal, sand and lava; give lava/arc/hotspot basalt ~2-3x and take carbonate/evaporite out), and retry a regolith-residence ceiling. It is cheap to compute, but it moves the CO2 balance, so re-measure together with PCO2_BALANCE (audit #2), not separately.
items.verify_reason: earth.py:103 sets supply = sim.weathered * land. earth.py:720 sets weathered = removed except under ice, with no lithology or saturation term; grep finds no saturation. docs/wiki/decisions.md:33 still lists 'smooth saturating law · PW-574', while the PW-574 ticket says 'Superseded by PW-576 option C' (status done, milestone v2). The stale ruling row is a real doc mismatch. A lithology-blind sink is a crude simplification; GEOCARB-style models weight basalt and drop carbonates and evaporites. It matters because the star calibration was tuned against this sink.

items.title: Continental volcano summits are capped at 3500 m above sea level, so Andean or Kilimanjaro-class volcanoes can't exist and arc cones on high plateaus are cut below their own ground
items.evidence: volcanism.py:60 TOP_MAX = (4200.0, 3500.0) '# m: highest summit at sea (Mauna Kea), on a continent'. It applies to active arc volcanoes too (volcanism.py:373-376: cut = top - TOP_MAX[cont]) and to extinct ones (:385). In stored worlds, active arc volcanoes pile up at the cap: 45/234 (067778), 56/491 (1df1c3), 106/657 (6909cb) have top_m in 3490-3510. On ground above 2 km the median cone relief is 158 m (1df1c3). Several active volcanoes have a summit below their floor (6 in 1df1c3, 6 in 6909cb). highlights.py:1158 stratovolcano() promises 'Chimborazo, Ojos del Salado', which are 6.3 and 6.9 km.
items.why_it_matters: Earth has dozens of continental volcanoes above 5 km (Ojos del Salado 6893, Chimborazo 6263, Cotopaxi 5897, Kilimanjaro 5895, Elbrus 5642, Orizaba 5636, Damavand 5610). What limits a volcano physically is its relief above its surroundings (edifice strength, flexure), not an absolute summit height. High volcanic plateaus (Altiplano peoples, puna herding, freeze-dried foods) are a recognisable culinary setting, and the volcano highlight is currently impossible to satisfy.
items.recommendation: Turn the continental cap into a relief cap (summit minus floor, ~4-5 km, Kilimanjaro's ~4.9 km relief as the upper end) and keep the oceanic 4.2 km absolute cap, which is physically sound (oceanic flexure). A one-line change in volcanism.py, plus re-checking the highlights' ties and the goldens.

items.title: End-of-run worlds sample the run's most sclerotic tectonics: one plate often covers 40-68% of the planet (Earth's largest, the Pacific, ~20%), and PW-565 is parked in v2
items.evidence: Stored worlds, largest plate's share of the surface: 067778 (892 Myr) 0.68, 119973 (800) 0.58, a12762 (972) 0.54, c00ebf (552) 0.53, dad91b (860) 0.50, 607540 (692) 0.49, d14b89 (892) 0.42; median ~0.37 over 18 worlds; only 4-8 plates above 1% on several. Earth: Pacific 103 Mkm2, ~20% (Bird 2003). PW-565 (milestone v2): stress rifts fall from 10-16 to 1-5 per 200 Myr after ~600 Myr, ridge length -40%, floor ages to 60-120 Myr. The 2026-10-24 ruling (decisions.md: default worlds at the run end) puts every default world in exactly that late phase. Nothing measures plate sizes: tools/scorecard.py has no plate-size metric, and world.py:316 reports summary 'plates' as max id + 1 (067778 says 'plates: 70' with 8 plates present). A compounding factor: isostasy.ocean_depth is half-space to 121 Myr (6.4 km), where the plate/GDH1 fits flatten at ~5.6-5.9 km, so an ageing ocean's sea-level fall is exaggerated by ~0.5-0.8 km of floor depth on old floor.
items.why_it_matters: Fewer, larger plates mean fewer active margins: fewer arcs, young ranges, rifts, porphyry and epithermal ore belts and volcanic soils, and longer stable coasts. The v1 'real enough for an amateur geologist' bar notices a planet two-thirds one plate. Moving default worlds to the run end turned a v2 curiosity into the state every default world shows.
items.recommendation: Re-rank PW-565 for v1 or record an explicit owner acceptance. Add a 'largest plate share' and 'plates >1%' diagnostic to scorecard (Earth anchor: largest ~20%, ~7-8 plates above 2%). Fix world.py:316 to count distinct plates. When PW-565 is worked, consider a plate-model (Parsons-Sclater/GDH1) flattening of ocean_depth, so ageing oceans don't over-drain the sea.

items.title: The setup's inherited crust ages ignore the run's length and the star anchor, so runs longer than ~1.6 Gyr end with crust older than the planet
items.evidence: setup.py:156-162: cratons 2500 + 900*a_n Myr and belts 850 + 500*a_n Myr at t = 0 (floored at 300), whatever the run's length. Stored ~0.8-1.0 Gyr worlds read continental crust_age up to 3715-3856 Myr (067778, 119973, 1df1c3), so the start's oldest is ~2.9-3.0 Gyr. Under the 2026-10-24 anchor (decisions.md; a run of length T spans star ages 4570-T to 4570), a 2 Gyr run starts on a 2.57 Gyr-old planet but with cratons already ~3 Gyr old, ending ~4.9-5 Gyr old, older than the Sun. make.py allows up to 4000 Myr (star-anchor audit #11). resources.py keys BIF (ramp 1800-2700, :594), diamonds (2000-2800, :621) and fantasy mithril (3000-3500, :680) on these ages. The star-anchor audit covers heat_start (#15) but not crust ages. The continental_start comment (params.py:17-20, 'land emerges over the first Gyr, as Earth's probably did') also assumes a young-planet start the anchor no longer gives for runs up to 2 Gyr.
items.why_it_matters: It is harmless for the v1 default 1 Gyr (start at 3.57 Ga, oldest crust ~3.9 Ga, plausible). But it is exactly the 'built on a hidden assumption' class: the 2 Gyr showcase/climate-window runs and PW-557 extensions get impossible ages, which the resource rules and any age-quoting lineage text would repeat.
items.recommendation: Fold into PW-813, which already adds the run-end parameter: scale or clip the inherited ages to the planet's age at the start (4570 - T, minus a few hundred Myr for the first crust). For T beyond ~3 Gyr, start with fewer and younger cratons. Note in PW-557 that an extension must not re-age the setup's crust.
items.verify_reason: setup.py sets ages of 2500+900*a_n for cratons and 850+500*a_n for belts, whatever the run's length. Stored worlds near 0.9 Gyr reach crust_age 3715-3948 Myr, so cratons start near 3.0 Gyr. make.py:113 allows runs up to 4000 Myr. Under the end-anchored star, a 2 Gyr run would end with crust older than the 4.57 Gyr system. It is harmless at the 1 Gyr default: the oldest crust ends near 3.9 Ga, close to Acasta's ~4.0 Ga. The low severity is right.

items.title: The breakup rule forbids rifting off continental pieces of 0.3-3% of the surface, the size class of India, Arabia, Zealandia, Greenland and Australia
items.evidence: events.py:186-191 piece_ok: a rift is refused if either side carries continent between 0.1*rift_min_piece and rift_min_piece of the surface (params.py:157-160 rift_min_piece 0.03, i.e. 1.5-15 Mkm2). The docstring says 'Rifts break continents into a few large pieces, not slivers'; overview §2.2 item 4 and the 2026-10-13/14 owner design decision (overview.md:113 'chose the breakup fix (minimum continental piece...)'). Gondwana's breakup made several pieces in that band: India ~0.9%, Arabia ~1%, Zealandia ~1%, Australia ~1.7%, Antarctica ~2.7%. A counterpoint: stored worlds still have 0-3 landmasses in the 0.3-3% band (Earth world 506694: 3), so the visible effect on landmass counts is modest, because such pieces can still form by margin subduction and sea level.
items.why_it_matters: The rule fixed over-fragmentation, but its premise that real breakup yields only a few big blocks is false. It removes the drifting-subcontinent story (India crossing an ocean to raise a Tibet) and isolated mid-size continents, which are where distinctive endemic fauna and cuisines come from. That is a v2 'fun' matter more than a v1 physics bar.
items.recommendation: Leave it for v1. File a needs-decision ticket: lower the band to ~0.3-1% or make it a rising hazard penalty rather than a hard refusal, and measure the rifted-piece size distribution over 6-10 seeds against Gondwana's.
items.verify_reason: events.py piece_ok refuses a rift when either side carries continent between 0.1 and 1 times rift_min_piece (0.03, params.py:155) of the surface. That is 1.5-15 Mkm2, which takes in India, Australia (about 1.5%) and Antarctica (about 2.7%). The rule is a documented owner design choice that fixed over-fragmentation, and the auditor notes such pieces still form by other routes. Its premise is still factually off. Low severity and leaving it for v1 is right.

items.title: Coal forms wherever vegetation cover is above 0.5, not only where coal-forming wetland forests exist
items.evidence: earth.py:754-756: swamp = land & (e < 250) & (P > 1000) & (sim.veg > 0.5); coal = swamp * coal_rate * dt. The docstring (:737-738) says 'if plants exist (none before land plants ~450 Ma on Earth)'. resources.py:96 PEAT_TREE 30 for the resource rule. Under PW-807's real calendar, land plants arrive at 470-500 Ma, but peat-forming woody swamp floras (and so coal) begin ~360 Ma, and the Carboniferous was the main coal age; moss/herb cover of 0.5 isn't a coal swamp.
items.why_it_matters: It is a small window (~110-140 Myr of run time) in which the run would lay coal on bare-ish lowlands. Coal is a fuel good for peoples (land.py 'coal' districts), and the coal rank and the oil/gas windows inherit its burial history.
items.recommendation: When PW-807 lands, gate coal on the arrival of the woody or wetland-forest plant group (vegetation.unlocked_at) rather than on veg > 0.5, and use the resource rule's tree cover in the run too. One line, folded into PW-807's scope.
items.verify_reason: earth.py:755 gates coal on sim.veg > 0.5, and veg is ground_cover. vegetation.py:1411 adds 0.6*nu for moss and ground cover, so a moss-only flora can pass 0.5 with no trees. The core code claim holds. It is partly overstated: today's compressed flora (PW-636) has no real calendar yet. PW-807 (v1, todo) already lists 'no coal before ~360 Ma' as an expected outcome, so the issue is a missing implementation detail inside a planned ticket, not a hidden assumption. The earliest coals are Devonian (~390 Ma), so the window is even smaller than stated. Fold it into PW-807.

items.title: The 3 C random climate drift is a temperature offset, not a carbon perturbation, so the CO2 thermostat works against it: in this model warm eras have low CO2, the reverse of Earth's record
items.evidence: planet/tectonics/earth.py global_temperature: target = drift + co2_term + albedo + star (lines ~281-283). The drift is an OU walk, sd climate_drift = 3 C over 40 Myr (params.py), described as standing in for 'all the carbon-cycle and ocean details this model doesn't have'. The weathering sink reads the local temperature (weathering(): exp(0.09 (T-15))), so a warm drift raises weathering and draws CO2 down. With WEATHER_K 0.09, WEATHER_CO2 0.4 and 3 C/doubling, the steady state is ln X = -0.225 dT, so roughly half of any non-CO2 warming is cancelled by lower CO2. Measured on the four showcase runs' keyframes after 300 Myr (runs/<id>/run.json stats; read-only snippet): for d30069 / 6c652c / 99dc70 / feaade, corr(global T, ln pCO2) = 0.27 / 0.18 / 0.75 / -0.08; sd of the non-CO2 part (drift+star+ice) = 3.6 / 3.6 / 3.0 / 3.4 C, against the CO2 term's 2.5 / 2.9 / 3.6 / 1.9; corr(CO2 term, rest) = -0.44 / -0.67 / -0.11 / -0.61; pCO2 below 180 ppm 7 / 19 / 32 / 22% of the time; 5th percentile 72-148 ppm, below Earth's Phanerozoic minimum (~180 ppm at glacial maxima). On Earth, Phanerozoic temperature and CO2 are strongly and positively coupled (Foster et al. 2017; Rae et al. 2021). PW-368 and docs/review/ice-v2-criteria.md A10 discuss the drift only as the cause of deep cold eras, never its sign effect on CO2. The star audit covers the same mechanism for the star term only.
items.why_it_matters: The things the drift stands in for (outgassing pulses, weatherability changes, organic burial) act on CO2 in reality. Applied as a temperature term, they give warm, CO2-starved worlds. Plants read the real pCO2 (PW-646), and PW-806/808 showed that tree cover depends on it. The showcase picker favours warm moments (PW-700), so default worlds land disproportionately on warm drift excursions with suppressed CO2. That is the treeless-tropics problem from a second source that the star anchor will not remove. For the culinary goal, a Cretaceous- or Eocene-like warm world should be lush and high-CO2, not a C4 grassland.
items.recommendation: Move the drift into the carbon cycle: a multiplicative OU noise on the volcanic source (or on weatherability) with the same 40 Myr memory, its sd re-picked so the dT spread stays ~3 C. Warm eras then come with high CO2 and cold eras with low CO2, as on Earth. Keep a much smaller pure-temperature residual only if it is needed (ocean and cloud states). Measure corr(T, ln pCO2) and the pCO2<180 share before and after, together with the star-anchor re-derivation (PW-812/815), since both change the same balance. File as a needs-decision draft: it changes every run.

items.title: The time zoom's co2_share 0.5 gives a glacial maximum ~0.47x the interglacial pCO2 (Earth: ~0.68x), so the zoom's plants see ~130 ppm at an LGM
items.evidence: planet/timezoom/params.py:112 co2_share = 0.5 'the share of that cooling that is CO2 (Earth's LGM ~half)'. forcing.py:92 co2 = co2_share * (-I*cool); plants.py:169 pco2 = pco2_0 * 2^(co2_c/co2_sens). On Earth, glacial_cool is 6.5 C, so the CO2 part is -3.25 C, i.e. 2^(-1.08) = 0.47x. From 280 ppm that is ~132 ppm; from the 142-160 ppm star-world slices it is ~70 ppm, which hits vegetation's CO2_RANGE floor (124 ppm, vegetation.py:233). With the cap (1.6x, e.g. zoom 606a1b at 10.4 C) it is 0.30x. Earth's LGM was 185-190 ppm against 280 (0.68x, -0.56 doublings), which at the model's own 3 C/doubling is -1.7 C, ~26% of 6.5 C. The 'about half' figure in the literature is greenhouse gases together (CO2+CH4+N2O ~2.8 W/m2) against ice and vegetation albedo (~3+ W/m2) (Hansen et al. 2008; Köhler et al. 2010). CO2 alone, 5.35 ln(190/280) = -2.1 W/m2, is about a third of the LGM forcing.
items.why_it_matters: The time zoom is the v1 'world you can zoom into', and its plant frames feed the forest-to-tundra test (PW-645), refugia (vegetation_glacial in the zoom meta) and the glacial 'now' option. A glacial at 130 ppm or less pushes C3 plants toward starvation far beyond what the LGM did (the LGM kept large forests, Prentice et al. 2011, as PW-806 cites). Glacial-era biomes and refugia (and any people whose foodways are set in a glacial) are then too treeless and too C4.
items.recommendation: Set co2_share so that the zoom's pCO2 ratio at I=1 matches Earth's LGM on Earth (~0.25-0.3 of glacial_cool at 3 C/doubling). Better: express it directly as a glacial pCO2 ratio (~0.68 at Earth's cooling, scaled with the cooling) so it no longer depends on co2_sensitivity. Fix the comment. Re-run the forest-to-tundra multi-seed test, since a smaller CO2 drop moves F.

items.title: The model's own Earth has 3% hot desert and 2% tropical rainforest (real ~14-20% and ~10-14%), and no v1 check or milestone covers it
items.evidence: worlds/506694.txt (Earth, model vs observed, 2026-10-23): hot desert 4.8%, tropical rainforest 2.7%, savanna 17.3%. 577526: 3.3 / 1.9%. Biome rule climate.py:2056-2087: hot desert needs T >= 18 C and p < 350 mm, so the model's Sahara/Arabia/Australia get more than 350 mm. The v1 sign-off notes it ('Even the model's Earth has very little rainforest and hot desert ... A reader will notice it on every world'), but the owning tickets PW-228 (vegetation agreement stuck at ~44%, regional rain: Sahel, India, Congo) and PW-290 (L7 ~10 points more arid than L6) have milestone null, and PW-015 (moisture transport) is blocked in v2. The v1 bar (icehouse share, hellhole, wet-tropics trees) does not test subtropical deserts at all.
items.why_it_matters: The v1 definition is 'passes muster to an amateur geologist or hydrologist'. With Earth's real geography the model makes no Sahara and almost no Amazon/Congo, the first thing such a reader checks. For the culinary north star, the desert/oasis, pastoral and rainforest foodways (dates, camel and goat pastoralism, tuber and forest-gathering cultures) are exactly the contrasts the ethnography needs. Desert-belt rainfall is the base climate, not a plant calibration.
items.recommendation: Put PW-228 (at least its subtropical-dryness part) in the v1 milestone, or record an explicit owner ruling that v1 ships with it. Add a diagnostic to the Earth check: hot-desert share and the 15-30 deg land precipitation of the model's Earth against GPCC (already in tools/earth_data.py). Look first at why the descending subtropical branch rains above 350 mm (the rain kernel's recycling or storm spread at 20-30 deg) before touching the biome thresholds.

items.title: The v1 ice-age bar ('cycles at ~100 kyr without runaway') is met by construction: the glacial index scripts the 100 kyr period, and the cooling it scripts varies 4x between similar Earth-likes
items.evidence: decisions.md 2026-10-20 'Run moments · v1 bar is "cycles at ~100 kyr without runaway"' (PW-492). timezoom/params.py: glacial_kyr = 100 (the ending bar falls to bar_lo at 100 kyr), backstop = 2x. orbit.py orbit_at hard-codes the eccentricity periods (cos(2 pi t/100.0), cos(2 pi t/405.0)): they are not TZParams, so every planet has Earth's Jupiter/Venus-set periods. cycle.cooling(): cooling = 6.5 C x (ice-free land poleward of the snowline / 0.035), capped at 1.6x. Stored showcase zooms (runs/*/run.txt 'Glacial index'): 41a7a4 3.2 C, 606a1b 10.4 C (cap), 6e96d2 3.8, ddc091 5.8, f06bbb 2.4, f778ab 3.7, fc82c2 7.9, fd187b 2.5. Five of eight are paced by summer sun at 73-80 S. PW-536 found a moment with 0.49 C (so effectively no ice age) because its polar land was already iced. Earth's 100 kyr rhythm is only the last ~1 Myr; before the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (~1.2-0.8 Ma) cycles were ~41 kyr. README.md:145 also lists a knob `insol_k` that TZParams no longer has (insol_gain/orbit_resp).
items.why_it_matters: Passing a bar the script guarantees is not evidence that the ice-age physics works, yet the owner may read it as 'ice ages work'. The share rule means that whether an Earth-like world gets real ice ages depends on whether its polar land is already ice-covered, which contradicts the owner ruling 'for Earth-like worlds NO ice ages is a fail' (PW-780) in the time zoom even when the run passes. Glacial depth (2.4-10.4 C) sets glacial refugia and sea-level land bridges, which matter for peoples' migrations.
items.recommendation: Label the cycle period as scripted in the README, the glossary and the v1 sign-off, and state the bar honestly as 'the scripted cycle runs without runaway'. Move the 100/405 kyr periods into TZParams. Before v1, at least floor the glacial cooling (e.g. count the land already under ice in the share, or give the CO2 part, which is global ocean carbon, no dependence on snowline land), so an Earth-like icehouse moment never gets ~0.5 C. The full fix is PW-470/PW-538 (v2). Fix the README's insol_k.

items.title: The ice-albedo rule still claims Earth's LGM as its anchor, though PW-449 showed it gives about half Earth's LGM feedback; the star and drift then decide whether ice ages happen
items.evidence: params.py: ice_albedo 1.5 C per 3%, ice_albedo_max 3.0 '... levelling off toward this many C (Earth's LGM ice sheets: ~2.5-3)'. earth.py albedo(f) = 3 tanh(1.5 f/0.03/3). Today's 3.1% already spends 1.43 C, so going to the LGM's ~8% gives +1.2 C. Köhler et al. 2010 put land-ice albedo at ~-3.2 W/m2, about -2.6 C at the model's 0.81 C per W/m2. PW-449 (wontdo) states this; PW-453 (v2) found no physical rule that keeps both Earth's zoom and the run's cold eras. The tanh's rationale ('a sheet spreading shades its own cold surroundings') runs the wrong way for equatorward growth, which gets more sun per km2 (PW-449's own note). docs/overview.md §2.8 says only 'levelling off toward 3 °C'. The time zoom copies the same rule (PW-445).
items.why_it_matters: The ice-albedo feedback is what makes icehouses and ice ages bite. At half strength, getting ice-but-not-icebox worlds is left to the 3 C random drift and the chosen star rate: the 0.45 star and the 500 ppm balance were picked on icehouse share with this weak feedback in place. If the feedback is ever corrected, those picks move. That is a compensating-kludge stack the owner should know about before signing v1 numbers.
items.recommendation: Correct the comment and the overview now ('tuned; about half Earth's LGM land-ice albedo forcing; PW-453'). Note in the star re-pick tickets (PW-812/815) that the icehouse-share calibration is conditional on this weak feedback. When PW-453 is taken up, re-pick star_brightening and PCO2_BALANCE in the same lane rather than separately.

items.title: PCO2_REF 350 treats the 1960-2000 observed climate as the equilibrium climate of 350 ppm; at the model's 3 C/doubling that equilibrium is ~300 ppm
items.evidence: climate.py:47 PCO2_REF = 350 'the CO2 of the climate model's dT = 0, Earth's climate as its data show it (~1960-2000, 320-370 ppm)'. earth.co2_term is an equilibrium mapping, dT = 3 log2(pCO2/350). The 1961-1990 climate the model is fitted to was ~0.3 C above 1850-1900 while CO2 was 315-355 ppm: a transient state, not equilibrium. The equilibrium CO2 for +0.3 C over the 280 ppm preindustrial is ~280 x 2^(0.1) ~ 300 ppm, ~0.67 C of forcing below 350. vegetation.CA_REF = PCO2_REF ('plants' today') inherits the same offset, though Earth's mapped vegetation grew mostly under 280-320 ppm. Also, earth.py co2_term's docstring says PCO2_BALANCE 'is a doubling warmer' than the reference; 500/350 is half a doubling (+1.5 C), as climate.py itself says.
items.why_it_matters: Small (~0.7 C, ~50 ppm), but it is the reference the star-anchor work is about to target ('re-derive so that a present-Sun end lands in Earth's plausible pCO2 range', star audit #2). Aiming the end of a run at 280 ppm on this mapping lands ~1 C colder than the climate the model's dT = 0 was fitted to.
items.recommendation: State dT = 0 as 'Earth's ~1961-1990 climate, in equilibrium at ~300 ppm', and either set PCO2_REF ~300 or keep 350 with the caveat recorded where PW-812/815 pick the end-of-run CO2 target. Fix co2_term's 'a doubling warmer' docstring. Re-check PW-806's 280-ppm forest test against the chosen reference.

items.title: The hellhole lines (median dT > 10.5 or max > 15.5 C) would fail Earth's own Eocene and PETM, both lush, forested climates
items.evidence: docs/review/base-climate/v2-climate-1/passrate2.py:24 hell = med > 10.5 or mx > 15.5. These are used in the v1 sign-off and PW-780 ('the first hellhole has appeared: 957317 ... +10.5 / 15.5'). Inglis et al. 2020 (Clim. Past 16, 1953): EECO GMST 27.0 C (23.2-29.7), ~10-16 C above preindustrial; PETM 31.6 C (27.2-34.5), ~+17. Scotese et al. 2021 gives a Phanerozoic GAT of up to ~36 C. In the run, model dT tracks area-mean temperature at roughly 0.95:1 (stored worlds: dT -5.8 -> 7.75 C mean, +6.5 -> 19.5 C). The owner's v1 language is 'molten hellhole'. Polar forests and crocodiles in the Arctic are documented for the EECO (Jaramillo et al. 2010, cited in PW-806).
items.why_it_matters: The label shapes rulings: the owner deciding 'a 2 Gyr run's late window has a hellhole' may reject or re-tune for a world that is Eocene-like, not molten. A greenhouse world is a valid and culinarily interesting Earth-like (polar forests, wide tropics), unlike a runaway greenhouse. The real habitability limits are tropical heat stress and water, not a global-mean line.
items.recommendation: Rename the class 'hothouse beyond Earth's record' and anchor its line at Earth's warmest well-dated states (e.g. median > ~+13, max > ~+18-20 C, PETM/Early Triassic), or replace it with a habitability measure (share of land whose warmest month exceeds a heat-stress or wet-bulb limit). Put it to the owner as a threshold question with the Inglis numbers, since thresholds are the owner's.

items.title: Sea level counts the ice part at full eustatic size but scales the ocean-basin part by hydro-isostasy (0.69): an inconsistent pair on Myr steps
items.evidence: earth.py global_temperature: the basin part uses rise = (rho_m - rho_w)/rho_m x the floor's shallowing, 'the water displaced also loads the floor'. update_climate: sea_ice = -0.9 x ice volume / ocean area, with no matching unloading of the ocean floor when water goes into ice, although the run's icehouses last tens of Myr (equilibrium). isostasy.py ocean elevations are fixed relative to a constant water load, and simulation.py subtracts sea_level directly. Removing a water layer d lets the floor rise rho_w/rho_m x d ~ 0.31 d, so relative sea level against the continents falls ~0.69 d.
items.why_it_matters: The run's icehouse sea levels (and the 20 m icehouse threshold, the -150/-430 m deep-ice criteria in tools/ice_criteria.py) are ~1.45x too large as freeboard changes against continents. That exaggerates how much shelf is exposed in cold eras (land bridges, coastal fishing grounds) and makes the criteria a mix of eustatic and freeboard units.
items.recommendation: Either apply the same 0.69 factor to the ice part in the run's freeboard (keep the eustatic figure as a diagnostic), or document that both parts are reported as eustatic and drop the 0.69 from the basin part. Thresholds in ice_criteria then need a note on which they mean. The time zoom (kyr) can keep the eustatic value, since ocean-floor GIA is only partial there.

items.title: Culinary water goods (fish runs, salt licks, salt routes, lake fisheries, predator-free islands) use thresholds in grid-dependent units, so L6 and L7 copies of the same planet get different foods
items.evidence: planet/lineages/seafood.py:54 RUN_FLOW = 3.0, :46 LICK_FLOW = 2.0, :55 RUN_LOSS = 0.96 'per cell upstream', :59 LAKE_CELLS = (1, 6) cells, :53 SHELF_M 'coastal sea cells (60 km)'; planet/lineages/salt_reach.py:20 RIVER_FLOW = 2.0; planet/coastform.py:93 ISLAND_CELLS = 3. All of these are in raw 'flow' units, which are cells x m/yr (planet/world.py:130, store.py:301). The default level is 6 (planet/make.py:93). Converting with hydrology.discharge: RUN_FLOW 3 is about 296 m3/s at L7 (3,113 km2 cells) and about 1,180 m3/s at L6 (12,450 km2 cells). A fish run's upstream decay of 0.96 per cell halves over about 1,000 km at L7 and about 2,000 km at L6. A 3-cell 'island free of land predators' is about 9,000 km2 at L7 and 36,000 km2 at L6. lineages/crossing.py:113 already uses a quantile, so it doesn't depend on the level; these don't. No ticket found (grep RUN_FLOW / 'cells of runoff' in issue-tracking: none).
items.why_it_matters: Fish, salt and sea-mammal access are core inputs to the culinary goal (who fishes, who trades salt). At the default L6, only rivers above about 1,200 m3/s get any anadromous run, and only rivers above about 800 m3/s count as salt-route rivers. The same seed's peoples eat differently at the showcase level than at the test level. Also, 300 m3/s is far above real salmon/shad rivers, which are often tens of m3/s.
items.recommendation: Convert to physical units: m3/s via hydrology.discharge (or catchment km2) for RUN_FLOW, LICK_FLOW and RIVER_FLOW; an e-folding distance in km for RUN_LOSS; km2 for LAKE_CELLS and ISLAND_CELLS; and the actual cell spacing for SHELF_M. Pick the run threshold from a catchment-size argument, not 3 cells. Check with one seed at L6 and L7 that fish_run and salt_lick shares agree to within noise. File it as an inbox draft (lineages + hydrology).

items.title: Rivers run 2-4x Earth's discharge, and the docs say the runoff ratio is Earth-like; nothing in the water outputs tracks it
items.evidence: docs/review/base-climate/v1-finish/step2/earth_check.txt:196-210 (latest): land runoff/rain 0.49 against Earth's 0.35-0.40 (0.38 with GPCC rain). Model/observed discharge: Amazon 1.83, Congo 3.74, Mississippi 3.59, Yenisei 2.67, Mackenzie 2.68, Murray 3.64, Nile 31.3. With GPCC rain the same routing gives Amazon 1.03 and Mackenzie 1.02, so most of the excess is the model's land rain (PW-015, blocked: ~1150 against 791 mm). Stored worlds (read-only scan of all 20 in worlds/): land R/P 0.45-0.54 and land P 890-1300 mm; every world's largest river is 150k-785k m3/s (Amazon 209k; 81aced 785k, 7082f5 530k); the Earth worlds 506694 and 577526 show an Amazon of about 390k m3/s. docs/overview.md:277 says runoff is '~40% of the rain on Earth's land', which only holds with observed rain.
items.why_it_matters: Every water-derived layer takes discharge at face value. These include river_nav depth (0.27 Q^0.3, so ships are reached on smaller rivers), the floodplain share (vegetation.floodplain: log10(q/500), feeding alluvium soils, the 'richest ground', and fertile classes), irrigation (humanuse IRRIGATE_Q = 100 m3/s), the delta class (DELTA_Q), the outlet-valley cut 0.1 Q^0.7 (deeper cuts drain more lakes), and the fish runs above. The worlds read as wetter and more river-rich than Earth, but the docs present the water balance as calibrated.
items.recommendation: Don't retune the hydrology to compensate; the routing is sound on observed rain. Fix the overview line so it gives both numbers (0.49 model rain, 0.38 GPCC). Add the Earth-check discharge ratios, and the generated worlds' land R/P and largest-river discharge, to the scorecard as a reported diagnostic, so PW-015's fix shows up downstream. Note in PW-015 that the land-rain excess carries into rivers, soils' alluvium and human use.

items.title: No evaporation from river wetlands. The Sudd was treated as an 'artefact basin' and drained by an Earth-tuned slope threshold, so exotic rivers through dry country keep all their water
items.evidence: PW-121 and PW-110: MIN_SLOPE = 0.1 m/km (planet/hydrology.py:95) was chosen because 'on Earth the artefact basins sit at 0.09-0.11 m/km (Sudd 0.09 ...). With 0.08 the Sudd stays a closed lake and the Nile vanishes.' The Sudd is real: the White Nile loses about half its inflow to evapotranspiration there (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudd; UNEP https://hotspots.unepgrid.ch/site/sudd-swamp), and the Inner Niger Delta loses about 40% (24-48%; https://iahs.info/uploads/dms/16775.26-138-143-344-30-Mahe-et-al-corr.pdf). The model has no such sink. kernels.lakes charges open-water evaporation only on lake cells. vegetation.flooded/floodplain (vegetation.py:796-821) builds a flooded share of each cell for plants and soils, but nothing in hydrology charges it any evaporation. Result: with observed GPCC rain the model Nile is still 4.55x observed (earth_check.txt:209) and the Murray is 3.64x with model rain.
items.why_it_matters: The Earth fix replaced a real process (wetland water loss) with a threshold that removes the wetland basin, which is the 'kludge compensating another error' pattern. On generated worlds the same gap makes desert-crossing rivers (Nile-, Niger- or Okavango-like) carry their whole headwater runoff to the sea. That overstates oases, irrigation, navigation and delta building in exactly the dry regions where water decides the culinary picture.
items.recommendation: Charge each cell's flooded share (or its floodplain share) the open-water evaporation minus the land AET, as lakes already do (src - loss x flooded). Feed it from the flood months (seasonal_flow), and cap it at the inflow. Then re-run the Earth check and revisit MIN_SLOPE against generated basins rather than the Sudd; the Sudd should come out as a big wetland that halves the White Nile. File it as a hydrology needs-decision draft, because it reopens PW-121's basis.

items.title: Lakes are scarce on current worlds: the 0.1 m/km drain rule acts as an on/off switch for generated basins, and L7 worlds fall below the project's own lake envelope
items.evidence: PW-121: generated L6 basins cluster at depth/radius 0.07-0.14 m/km, 'so the rule is close to a switch for them'; it halved lake area. A read-only scan of the stored worlds gives lakes as a share of land: L7 0.07 (2a7385), 0.11, 0.12, 0.13, 0.15, 0.23, 0.25, 0.61, 0.98%; L6 0.16-0.91%. Most L7 worlds are below PW-054's 0.2% envelope and far below 'Earth's resolvable lakes ~0.7%' (PW-121 option C). Closed lakes: 1-114 cells. The outlet cut CHANNEL_K x Q^0.7 (hydrology.py:103; ~300 m at 100k m3/s) was tuned against Earth's drained lowlands, and here it runs on discharges 2-4x Earth's (previous finding). Tracked in part as PW-054 (high, todo) and PW-243.
items.why_it_matters: Lake fisheries (seafood fish_lake), salt lakes and playas (salt_lake, the salt-trade economy), wetlands and freshwater landmarks all come from these lakes. A v1 Earth-like world with about 0.1% lakes reads as unusually dry-floored to an amateur hydrologist, and the culinary layer loses a whole class of food and salt sources.
items.recommendation: Don't loosen the rule as a stopgap (owner ruling PW-121). Report lake share per level in the scorecard against the 0.7% resolvable-Earth figure. After the wetland-ET fix and the rain fix, re-measure whether MIN_SLOPE and CHANNEL_K still need their Earth-tuned values. Put the evidence on PW-054 so its v1 status is explicit.

items.title: BQART glacial factor is up to 5x too weak (1 + share instead of 1 + 0.09 x percent)
items.evidence: planet/coast.py:621: B = (0.6 + 1.4 x soft) x (1 + 1.0 x iced), with iced a 0..1 share, so the glacial term reaches at most 2. Syvitski & Milliman (2007) give I = 1 + 0.09 Ag with Ag the glaciated percentage, so a fully glaciated basin has I = 10 (CSDMS poster https://csdms.colorado.edu/csdms_wiki/images/Cohen_CSDMS_poster_small.pdf; paper https://website.whoi.edu/gfd/wp-content/uploads/sites/14/2018/10/syvitski__Milliman_2007_75324.pdf). The docstring (coast.py:108-111) cites the paper but not the coefficient. The lithology range 0.6-2.0 is also narrower than the paper's L (~0.5-3); worth checking against the paper.
items.why_it_matters: Glacier-fed rivers bring the most sediment per unit water on Earth (the Copper and Alaskan rivers, Himalayan rivers). Underweighting them changes the Galloway weights, the delta class (DELTA_KGS), turbidity plumes (coastal.river_turbidity), and through those kelp/seagrass light limits and the shellfish/fish layers on cold, glaciated coasts.
items.recommendation: Use I = 1 + 9.0 x iced share (the same as 0.09 x percent) and check L against the paper's table. Re-run tools/coast_check.py and goldens; it is a constant fix with no tuning.
items.verify_reason: coast.py:621 has B = (0.6 + 1.4 soft) x (1 + 1.0 iced), with iced a 0-1 share, so the glacial term is at most 2. Syvitski & Milliman 2007 define I = 1 + 0.09 Ag with Ag in percent, which gives up to 10 for a fully glaciated basin, and L runs about 0.5-3. The docstring (coast.py:108-111) cites the paper while the coefficient differs. It is a constant fix. The effect is limited to glaciated basins' sediment loads, delta class and turbidity, so it stays low.

items.title: The world erosion pass scales its stream-power constant by 2^(level-5) on top of sqrt(flow in cells), a scaling the implicit scheme doesn't call for
items.evidence: planet/hydrology.py:63: k = 0.018 x 1.6 x strength x 2 ** (grid.level - 5), comment 'finer cells -> more upstream cells'. kernels.stream_power (kernels.py:809-818) applies f = k sqrt(flow) as the implicit factor K A^m dt/dx. Since A = flow_cells x cell area and sqrt(cell area) ~ dx, K sqrt(A)/dx is already K' sqrt(flow_cells): the 'more upstream cells' effect is in sqrt(flow) itself. The extra factor doubles the per-pass cutting per level for the same physical river: 4x L6 at L7, where my derivation expects 2x. Used for every world (world.py:110). Unverified against measurement.
items.why_it_matters: It is a candidate cause of L7 worlds holding fewer lakes than L6 (previous finding), by cutting lake outlets and hollow rims more, and of level-dependent valley depths in the showcase level. It may be deliberate, but nothing documents it.
items.recommendation: Measure: run world erosion on the same keyframe resampled at L6 and L7 and compare valley depth and lake share. If the 2^(level-5) is not needed, remove it (goldens change on purpose). Otherwise write down why.

items.title: Discharge assumes equal-area cells; the Earth check corrects for this but the world and run code path doesn't
items.evidence: planet/hydrology.py:110-112 discharge() uses 4 pi R^2 / n per cell. Cell areas at L6/L7 range 0.67-1.21 x the mean (sd 8.5%; ocean.cell_area_km2 on shared_grid 6 and 7). tools/earth_check.py:556 scales the runoff by w / w.mean() (true areas) before routing, and worlds do not (world.py, rivers_and_lakes). seafood/coastal river_loads and humanuse use the same mean area.
items.why_it_matters: Small and medium rivers' discharge is off by up to about 20-30% depending on where they sit on the icosahedron. That is a pattern of the grid, not of climate, and it hits every m3/s threshold (navigation classes, irrigation, delta, fish runs). The Earth check therefore validates a slightly different computation than the one worlds use.
items.recommendation: Weight runoff by true cell area in rivers_and_lakes, lakes and erode (one place), and drop the earth_check special case.

items.title: Coastal life and river forms are not on the real calendar (PW-807): kelp, coral reefs and seals are ungated, and rivers meander before land plants
items.evidence: planet/coastal.py: kelp 'Brown algae: no plant-group gate', and reefs have no gate apart from reef_temp; coastform seals and seabirds are ungated; zoom_fine_meander and zoom_fine_floodplain make single-thread meandering rivers whatever the flora. Real dates: kelp forests (Laminariales) diversified ~30 Ma; scleractinian reefs date from ~240 Ma; pinnipeds ~25-30 Ma; before rooted land plants (~450 Ma) rivers were mostly braided sheet-flow without stable muddy floodplains (Gibling & Davies 2012, Nature Geoscience). Mangroves and seagrass are gated on TrBE and salt marsh on C3G, which PW-807 will move to the real dates.
items.why_it_matters: Default worlds are taken at the run end, so this is not a v1 blocker. But 'earlier eras by age before now' is now ruled (decisions.md 2026-10-24 Calendar), and those slices would show kelp, seals, modern reefs and meandering floodplains with alluvium soils hundreds of Myr too early.
items.recommendation: Add these to PW-807's gate list: kelp, pinnipeds, scleractinian reefs (an older reef builder before that), and a braided-only river style plus no mud floodplain or peat before land plants. Low effort once PW-807's end-counted calendar exists.

items.title: No groundwater at world scale: dry land away from rivers is 'no fresh water within reach', and soils' leaching water doesn't match the world's runoff
items.evidence: planet/humanuse.py fresh_water sources (analyse_world ~l.560): runoff >= 100 mm, q >= 20 m3/s, fresh lakes, flooded >= 20%, plus only foot-of-mountain springs (springs()); there are no aquifers or wells. hydrology.py:285-287 BASEFLOW 0.5 everywhere (FROZEN_BASEFLOW keyed to frozen months, not the soils' permafrost class). planet/soils.py:171 and :200-206 compute leaching with a fixed Fu w = 2.6 on annual totals, while the docstring claims it is 'as the climate's water balance'. The climate uses a vegetation-set w per cell and half-years (climate.py:1867-1895). soils CAP_SCALE / F_NORM (soils.py:182-185) are renormalised to Earth's land mean.
items.why_it_matters: Arid pastoralists and oasis farmers rely on wells and shallow aquifers (qanats, wadis, sand-river wells), which is a major culinary axis (herds, dates, irrigation). The world currently tells peoples that interior drylands have no water. The soils mismatch is small but makes leaching and weathering inconsistent with the world's own runoff layer.
items.recommendation: For v1, add a crude groundwater reach: alluvium, sandstone or coastal-plain aquifers recharged by upstream runoff give 'wells' fresh water within a few cells of wetter catchments. Feed soils' leaching from the climate's own runoff (or pass its w) instead of a fixed 2.6. File both as inbox drafts; neither needs new physics beyond what the layers already store.

items.title: PW-806's acclimation does move Earth, partly compensates the dim-tropics error (PW-808), and now gives the LGM more rainforest than today
items.evidence: v1-finish-9/README.md section 2 says 'No change at 350 ppm (so no change on Earth)', and section 5 says 'Earth barely moves, as intended'. Its own section 3 table shows Earth's model climate at 350 ppm going from 34.7 to 41.2% trees and from 41.6 to 60.8% wet-equatorial trees. veg_check_note.txt already has model tree cover at 0.34 against MODIS 0.19. The same README says 'What is left of the warming response comes from the base climate's dim tropics' (PW-808: GPP ~1350 against an observed 2300-3500), so the plant change is carrying part of a climate error. In its LGM-like case (185 ppm, -5 C) wet-equatorial trees are 72.3%, against 60.8% today. That contradicts the evidence the ticket itself cites (Harrison & Prentice 2003; Prentice et al. 2011: low CO2 on its own shrank glacial forests). The parameters were taken at or near the top of the literature: RESP_ACCLIM = 0.8 (vegetation.py:140; trait data ~0.5, Reich 2016 is the high end), stacked on CUE conservation and PS_ACCLIM 0.5. ACCLIM_SPAN went from 6 to 10 C after looking at results (vegetation.py:145). The guarding desert test ended at 0.295 against a < 0.3 bound. PW-806 is marked done although its in-run checkbox is unmet.
items.why_it_matters: When PW-808 brightens the tropics, the stacked acclimation will likely overshoot forest. The time zoom's glacial-refugia story, which drives where peoples and crops sit through the last 30 kyr, loses its CO2 signal: glacial maxima look as forested as interglacials.
items.recommendation: Correct the README and ticket wording. Reopen PW-806, or make PW-808 its acceptance gate. Add an ordered check to the plant tests: LGM-like (185 ppm, colder, drier) has less tropical forest than Holocene 280 ppm, and 280 ppm has slightly less than 350 ppm. Re-test RESP_ACCLIM at the trait-data 0.5 once PW-808 is fixed, and keep 0.8 only if the anchors still need it.
items.verify_reason: 'No change at 350 ppm' in README section 2 describes only change 1 (CUE held at today's value), and that is literally true. 'Earth barely moves' in section 5 refers to veg_check: forest 43.6 -> 43.6 Mkm2, agreement 62.1 -> 61.6. So the wording is not false. It does sit badly beside section 3, where Earth's model climate goes 34.7 -> 41.2% trees and 41.6 -> 60.8% wet-equatorial trees. That inconsistency is real and should be reconciled. LGM above today: the old code already had 185 ppm at -5 C at 42.0 against today's 41.6, and 280 ppm at -4 C at 70.2. Cooling raising tropical forest is therefore a pre-existing property of the model climate (the hot, dim tropics). PW-806 amplified it but did not create it, and the README flags that rain held fixed overstates the LGM. RESP_ACCLIM = 0.8 is the top of the cited range, 0.295 against a < 0.3 test bound is tight, and the span change from 6 to 10 C is a documented judgement call. The ticket's done note explains that the in-run check waits for the star anchor. Adding the ordered LGM < Holocene <= today test, and gating on PW-808, are good recommendations.

items.title: The lineage calendar assumes Earth's Holocene (today's land for 10 kyr, farming from ~10 ka), but the world's 'now' can be 4 kyr after a glacial maximum
items.evidence: planet/lineages/history.py:47 HOLOCENE_KYR = 10 ('the land's living goods ... are today's from then on'), history.py:33 FARM_KYR = 6, spec.py:263 GROUP_KYR = 6. Crop and animal anchors are fixed Earth ka (crop_defs.py: wheat 10.5, rice 9, maize 9; animal_defs.py), jittered by animals.py JITTER 0.2. The present is finish.now_kyr('interglacial') (finish.py:80-121): the highest-sea-level frame of the latest low-glacial-index stretch, with nothing about how long that stretch has lasted. Read-only check on the v1 L7 showcase time zooms: 41a7a4 has its 'now' at 294 kyr with glacial index 0.87 at -10 kyr and 0.75 at -6 kyr, so the interglacial is 0 kyr old. fd187b's is ~8 kyr old, 606a1b ~10, ddc091 ~14 (and 606a1b's 'interglacial' sits at -120 m sea level).
items.why_it_matters: On 41a7a4, farming, the first domestications and 'today's farmland and pasture' all happen during the last deglaciation. Ice sheets and -100 m coasts are treated as present-day goods. Earth's causal link (agriculture after the climate stabilised in the Holocene) has been replaced by Earth's dates.
items.recommendation: Key the lineage epoch constants to the world's own deglaciation: t_term = the last time the glacial index fell below ~0.3 before 'now'. Set HOLOCENE_KYR, FARM_KYR and the domestication anchors relative to t_term, keeping the Earth offsets, or gate them on the glacial index. Separately, have now_kyr prefer interglacials at least ~8-10 kyr old, or report the age, and file the 606a1b -120 m 'interglacial' for the climate lane.
items.verify_reason: The mechanism is confirmed. HOLOCENE_KYR = 10 (history.py:47), FARM_KYR = 6 and GROUP_KYR = 6 are fixed, and now_kyr (finish.py) picks the highest-sea-level frame of the last stretch with index <= 0.05, with no check on how old that stretch is. Recomputing from runs/*/run.json: 41a7a4's 'now' is t=294, with index 0.87 at 286, 0.75 at 288 and 0.25 at 292, so its interglacial is about 0-2 kyr old. That is worse than stated, and real. The other three are fine: fd187b's index is below 0.3 from ~10 kyr before now, 606a1b's from ~12 kyr and ddc091's from ~16 kyr. So the problem hits one of four showcases, not the general case. 606a1b's -120 m 'interglacial', after a -311 m glacial, is a real oddity that belongs to the climate lane. Keying the epoch constants to the world's own deglaciation is the right fix.

items.title: Two domestication anchors are outdated archaeology: chickens at 8 ka and horses at 5.5 ka (Botai)
items.evidence: planet/lineages/animal_defs.py:131 has fowl anchored at 8.0 kyr. Peters et al. 2022 (PNAS) find no unambiguous chickens before ~1650-1250 BCE (~3.5 ka), domesticated on rice and millet farms in mainland SE Asia; the older ~8 ka northern-China claims were rejected (https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/tempting-rice.html). animal_defs.py:123 has horse at 5.5 kyr, the Botai date. Botai horses are Przewalski's lineage; modern domestic horses (DOM2) arose in the lower Volga-Don ~4.2 ka (Librado et al. 2021, Nature; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8550961). The CLIP of 0.7-1.5x is wide enough to land chickens before most staple crops.
items.why_it_matters: The culinary goal: chickens and eggs would spread through a world's farming peoples about twice as early as they should, and before the cereals that drew junglefowl in. The fast-contact horse rule (PW-794) starts more than a millennium early, which reshapes steppe history and horse-milk dairying.
items.recommendation: Set fowl to ~3.5 kyr and make its taming need a known grain crop (rice or millet) on the same land. Set horse to ~4.2 kyr for the riding and spreading lineage; optionally allow an earlier local horse-milking taming that does not spread. Cite the sources in the table comment.
items.verify_reason: animal_defs.py has fowl at 8.0 and horse at 5.5 (uptake='contact', speed 2.5), with JITTER 0.2 and CLIP 0.7-1.5 in animals.py:35. Peters et al. 2022 (PNAS) put the earliest unambiguous chickens at ~3.5 ka in Thailand, on rice and millet farms. Librado et al. 2021 put the spreading DOM2 horse at ~4.2 ka, and Botai horses are the Przewalski's lineage. Both are easy table fixes. The impact is modest: these are jittered anchors on a fantasy world, and the peoples layer sits outside the v1 physics bar. The chicken date does decide how far eggs have spread by the present.

items.title: No pigs (nor camelids, water buffalo, yak, reindeer, ducks or geese), while the brief promises salt pork
items.evidence: planet/lineages/animal_defs.py TABLE has only horse, dog, caprine, cattle and fowl among real animals; grep finds no pig or swine anywhere in planet/. Yet planet/lineages/brief.py:875 writes 'their halls cure and brine freely (salt pork, brined cheese, ...'. PW-691's owner note asked for 'the rest as many at a time as fits' after horses. No ticket tracks pigs.
items.why_it_matters: Pork and lard are central to East Asian, European, Pacific and Mesoamerican-contact cuisines. Pigs are forest-edge and household animals that need no pasture, so their absence biases the protein and fat mix toward grazing herds. In the fuels this shows as tallow and bone on open ground and nothing for forest farmers. Andean, Arctic and S-Asian cuisines lose their signature animals.
items.recommendation: Add a pig row (~10.5 ka; forest and woodland edge and farm villages; not taken up by pastoral nomads; lard as a fat). Rank camelid, buffalo, reindeer and duck rows as follow-ups. Until pigs exist, make the brief's salt-pork text conditional on a pig being known.
items.verify_reason: Verified. The TABLE's real animals are horse, dog, caprine, cattle and fowl only. grep finds no pig, swine, pork or lard in planet/ except brief.py:875's 'salt pork', and no ticket mentions pigs. PW-691's owner note does say 'add the rest as many at a time as fits'. This is a real gap for the culinary goal, though not for the v1 physics definition. The brief's text should be conditional on a pig being known until a pig row exists.

items.title: Before grasses, every herb and shrub niche falls back to moss; there are no ferns or horsetails, and groups are dated by first appearance rather than dominance
items.evidence: In vegetation.py:264 STANDINS, C3G, TunH, XerS and HthS fall back to ('Moss',) only, and TrBE/TeBS fall back to conifers. GROUPS (vegetation.py:245) has no fern, horsetail or lycopsid type. Type 61 (vegetation.py:433) reads 'moss and crust carpet ... no grass yet, the land before flowers'. In reality the Devonian-to-Paleogene ground layer was ferns, horsetails, lycophytes, cycads and seed ferns (fern prairies and fern savannas), and flowers had existed since ~130 Ma. The GROUPS fractions date first appearance. Angiosperms became dominant trees only ~100-66 Ma, and grass-dominated open habitats only ~40-20 Ma (Stromberg 2011); PW-807 itself notes 'dominant ~100', 'widespread ~55', 'spread ~8'. Grasses also unlock TunH 'graminoids and forbs', but forbs are angiosperm herbs present since the Cretaceous.
items.why_it_matters: Under PW-807's real calendar this governs roughly 375-70 Ma of every run: the Phanerozoic analogue whose ground cover sets erosion, weathering and the CO2 calibration. The owner also wants earlier eras on request ('slice --ago 70', a dinosaur-age setting), which would show moss carpets where there should be fern and cycad country.
items.recommendation: As part of PW-807, add one pre-angiosperm herb and shrub PFT ('ferns, horsetails and cycads', with C3G-like water use, low fire fuel and no grazing value) as the stand-in for C3G, TunH, HthS and XerS from ~385 Ma. Keep moss only before vascular plants. Date groups by when they became widespread, rename type 61 ('the land before vascular plants'), and add a 'fern and cycad country' type.
items.verify_reason: In vegetation.py STANDINS, C3G, TunH, XerS and HthS fall back to Moss only. No fern or horsetail PFT exists; the only pre-angiosperm vascular groups are WetH and the conifer group. The GROUPS fractions match first appearances: flowering trees at 0.73 x 470 Myr is ~127 Ma, grasses at 0.85 is ~70 Ma. Type 61's 'the land before flowers' is wrong between ~127 and 70 Ma, when flowering trees are already unlocked. Default worlds are taken at the run end with the full flora, so v1 is affected only through the run's pre-angiosperm ground cover, its weathering and CO2 history, and past slices. That makes this crude-sound for v1, but worth folding into PW-807 cheaply.

items.title: The run's plant weathering factor cites GEOCARB but is a 1.0-1.75x NPP term, so moss weathers like forest
items.evidence: planet/tectonics/earth.py:107-109 computes 'roots and soil CO2 speed it up ... (GEOCARB's biological weathering factor)' as plants = 1 + 0.5*clip(npp/800, 0, 1.5), which is at most 1.75x and depends only on NPP. GEOCARB III (Berner & Kothavala 2001) uses about a 4x vascular-plant effect over pre-vascular land (Moulton & Berner 1998; summarised at https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.04234), driven by fine roots, not by productivity. Algae and lichen cover weathers much more weakly. In the model, the Moss/Sph stand-ins (unlocked at plants_from) earn the same factor per unit NPP as trees.
items.why_it_matters: PW-807 makes the arrival of land plants a real event in long runs: the Devonian CO2 drawdown. Its size, and so the reference-freeze and CO2-balance questions in the star-anchor audit (#1, #2, #6), depend on this factor. A 1.75x cap tied to NPP understates the drawdown and gives the wrong groups credit.
items.recommendation: Either correct the comment ('crude, weaker than GEOCARB's ~4x') or make the factor depend on rooting: ~1 for moss and crust, rising with the tree and shrub cover of vascular groups, total effect ~2-4x. Measure it together with the star zero point and PW-807's CO2 check rather than tuning it separately.
items.verify_reason: tectonics/earth.py:107-109 is as quoted: plants = 1 + 0.5*clip(npp/800, 0, 1.5), at most 1.75x, citing 'GEOCARB's biological weathering factor'. GEOCARB uses a roughly 4x vascular-plant effect, with field estimates of about 2-10x (Moulton & Berner 1998). So the citation overstates the match, and the factor does not distinguish rooting. 'Moss weathers like forest' is overstated, though: the factor scales with NPP, so low-NPP moss and crust earns little. Only per unit NPP is it equal. How much this matters depends on how the weathering reference is set (star-anchor audit #1 and #2), so it should be measured together with those, as recommended.

items.title: gameattrs calls its values 'game numbers, not fitted', yet they drive peoples' subsistence, and pasture ignores forage quality
items.evidence: planet/gameattrs.py:12 says they are 'not fitted to anything: they are game numbers'. But lineages/land.py:265-266 turns grazing, foraging, timber and fuel into the land goods that set herders' and foragers' capacity and the fuels' graze input. Grazing (gameattrs.py:171) is herb NPP plus browse, saturating at 250 g C, with no forage-quality or soil-nutrient term. On 1df1c3, 'tropical grassland' at a median 1648 mm of rain scores grazing 4.21 against short-grass steppe's 3.83. Herbivore biomass actually peaks at intermediate rainfall on fertile soils, and tall wet C4 grass is poor forage (Olff, Ritchie & Prins 2002, Nature; Bell 1982). Foraging (gameattrs.py:174) counts game only as 0.16 x grazing, so forest game (deer, pig, primates) is roughly zero.
items.why_it_matters: Herding, dairying, dung fuel and hunter density are core to the culinary brief. Under this rule the wettest grasslands make the best pastoralist country and forests hold no game, so the herder and forager split is mis-placed on every world.
items.recommendation: Correct the docstring: these values are now model inputs. Add a forage-quality factor (a falling ramp with rain or moisture above ~1000 mm and with the C4 share, times soil fertility) and a browse and forest-game term to foraging. Check herder and forager placement on one remade world. Keep it crude, but make it the right shape.
items.verify_reason: gameattrs.py:12 says 'not fitted to anything: they are game numbers', while lineages/land.py:265-266 feeds grazing, foraging, timber and fuel into the land goods. Grazing is herb NPP plus 0.3 x shrub browse, saturating at 250, with only a snow and frost season term: no forage quality, no wetness penalty, no soil fertility. Foraging counts game only as 0.16 x grazing; mast is plant food, not forest game. The ecology is right: herbivore biomass peaks at intermediate rainfall on fertile soils (Olff, Ritchie & Prins 2002). 'Not fitted' is literally true, so the docstring is less wrong than claimed. The substantive point, that wet tall-grass country rates as the best pasture, holds. The 1df1c3 numbers (4.21 against 3.83) were not re-checked.

items.title: Two acknowledged temporary paths in the plants contradict the 'no temporary fixes' rule: the Earth-fitted GRAZE placeholder and crown fire switched off in runs
items.evidence: vegetation.py:843 has GRAZE = 0.05 ('placeholder for fauna: remove in PW-103'). PW-207 says it was added because the Great Plains and Eurasian steppe went to forest at 700-800 mm on Earth, and it applies on every world whether or not grazers exist; PW-207 is v2. tectonics/earth.py:320 runs vegetation.model(..., crown=False) with the comment '(crown fire, PW-347: not yet in runs)', and the docstring at vegetation.py's equilibrium says 'leave it off for now'. So the run's boreal vegetation, albedo and weathering use different fire physics from the finished world.
items.why_it_matters: GRAZE is an Earth-copied fix for a forest overshoot whose likely real causes are drought variability, fire and soil, and it hides that cause. The run and world mismatch means the run's keyframe tree cover, which warm-starts the world's and the time zoom's vegetation, differs from what the world model would produce.
items.recommendation: Turn crown fire on in runs, or record why not as a ruling. For GRAZE, either diagnose the 700-800 mm forest overshoot (fire weather, tree water cap) and remove it, or have the owner rule it a v1 approximation in decisions.md so it is no longer an unlogged stopgap.
items.verify_reason: GRAZE is not an unlogged stopgap. It is 'decision 8' in vegetation.py's comments, is tracked as PW-207 (v2), and decisions.md:63 rules fauna post-v1. It also already tapers with moisture: GRAZE*clip(1.5 - mi), with the comment 'none where it is wet all year'. The 'no temporary fixes' rule is about merging new partial fixes, not about long-standing tracked placeholders. Crown fire off in runs is documented at earth.py:320 and in the model docstring (vegetation.py:1020). The run and world fire-physics mismatch is real but minor, since the world re-equilibrates its own vegetation. Recording both as v1 approximations is cheap and sensible.

items.title: Crop wild and grown ranges use mean annual temperature and rain only, with no frost-free season or rain seasonality
items.evidence: In lineages/crop_defs.py _range, each crop is a window on env['temperature'] (annual mean) and annual precipitation; only olive and vine use the Koppen class. vegetation.site already computes gdd5, tc, tw, dry months and summer drought, but the crops do not read them. Examples: rice (wild MAT >= 16) is allowed in dry-summer Mediterranean climates with 900 mm of winter rain; spring wheat country at MAT ~0-3 (continental) and maritime places at the same MAT are treated alike.
items.why_it_matters: Where staples grow decides each people's cuisine. Annual means misplace summer crops (maize, rice, sorghum) and winter crops (wheat, barley) wherever the climate is strongly seasonal or continental.
items.recommendation: This is crude but cheap to improve: for summer annuals use warm-season temperature (tw or gdd) and warm-season rain; for winter cereals use tc and winter rain; reuse vegetation.site's indices. No new physics is needed.
items.verify_reason: crop_defs._range windows env['temperature'] and env['precipitation'] (annual), with optional Koppen classes, elevation, tree cover, soil and rice's flat-lowland term. It reads no season indices. The rice example is weak: irrigated rice really is grown in Mediterranean climates (the Po valley, Spain, Egypt), and the flat and wetland term stands in for that. The general point about summer and winter crops in seasonal or continental climates holds. It is crude but sound, and cheap to improve.

items.title: Farming, the 'Holocene' and the domestication dates follow Earth's calendar, not the world's own last deglaciation
items.evidence: planet/lineages/history.py:33 FARM_KYR = 6.0 (agricultural lines get 2x speed and a 0.5x rival load on farmland from then: lines 928, 945). history.py:47 HOLOCENE_KYR = 10.0 (from then farmland, pasture and coasts are 'today's': line 1115). animal_defs.py and crop_defs.py anchor every domestication to Earth's date (wheat 10.5, cattle 10.5, rice 9 kyr), jittered x0.7-1.5 (animals.py:43). None of this reads the world's climate. The showcase present, time zoom f778ab (runs/f778ab/run.json frames), is still in a glacial at 290 kyr: sea level -15 m, 17.7 C, ice_age 'building'. Its deglaciation only starts at ~294 kyr ('ending'), and global T jumps from 17.7 to 20.9 C over the last 6 kyr. So in this world '10 kyr ago' is a cold glacial with low sea level, yet the sim treats it as today's land and plants wheat there. run b69f51 run.txt also has foragers walking land bridges 'at low sea' ~10 kyr ago in the same window. A second sign: the 200-kyr 'human' line has way = 'farmer' and the 'agricultural' trait (seven_meals.toml, dnd.toml). It is the tamer for crops 190 kyr before farming exists, and FARM_KYR is the only thing that holds it back.
items.why_it_matters: The owner ruled that a run's end is 'now' and that default worlds are taken at the run end (PW-807). The agricultural revolution is the most climate-dependent event in the peoples history: on Earth it follows the Holocene's stable warmth (Richerson, Boyd and Bettinger 2001). Pinning it to Earth's 10.5 kyr is an Earth-copied clock. It can put the first fields in a glacial and the 'modern' land goods before the world's ice has gone. Every crop, herd, fuel and dairy line in the culinary brief sits on top of this.
items.recommendation: Measure the world's last termination from the time zoom (the frame where ice_age turns 'ending', or where sea level and temperature cross a threshold toward the present). Set HOLOCENE_KYR, FARM_KYR and the crop and herd anchors relative to it, e.g. first cultivation = termination age minus ~1 kyr, with the existing jitter. Gate the agricultural push and speed on the people actually knowing a staple crop (the crop pass already tracks this), not on the trait plus a fixed date. Draft a ticket and note it in docs/wiki/decisions.md as an extension of the PW-807 calendar ruling.
items.verify_reason: The cited code checks out. history.py:33 FARM_KYR=6.0, :47 HOLOCENE_KYR=10.0, :928/945 gate the agricultural speed-up on trait plus a fixed date, and :1115/_land_mult switches to the present-day land goods on a fixed clock. The f778ab frames confirm the world: t=290 kyr gives 17.69 C and sea level -15.4 m, warming starts at about 292 kyr, and it reaches 20.99 C at 300 (the b69f51 present is 300 kyr). So in this world 10 kyr ago is still glacial and the warm stable spell starts only ~2-6 kyr before the present. Capacity does read each step's temperature, which softens the effect but does not move the clock. Two things argue for medium rather than high. The peoples layer is milestone v2, not a v1 physics item. And the owner's PW-807 ruling deliberately puts plant groups on Earth's calendar counted back from the end, so an Earth clock is in line with existing rulings. What gets the clock wrong here is the ice-age kludge (PW-471), not the anchors themselves. The fix is still worth doing: anchor HOLOCENE_KYR and FARM_KYR to the world's own last termination. Minor point: land bridges at low sea ~10 kyr ago would also be plausible on Earth (about -40 m then), so that detail is weak evidence.

items.title: Population density ignores land productivity: 14 million tundra 'reindeer herders' with no reindeer, 107 million foragers
items.evidence: history.py:175-215 capacity(): K is only the people's comfort niche (temperature, rain, prefers). spec.py:118-130 says density is 'people per km² of full habitat (K = 1)'. The land goods multiply K but are renormalised to a mean of 1 over the people's country (spec Use docstring, history._land_mult), so a niche at full comfort has the same density anywhere. A group inherits its people's density. run b69f51 run.txt 'Numbers at the present': cervid_tundra 13,853,505 people at 2/km² on 10.29 Mkm² of tundra; human_forager 107,534,020 at 3/km² on 103.6 Mkm²; only 1.63% of the land is empty. Real ethnographic hunter-gatherer densities mostly run 0.01-1/km², and Arctic peoples ~0.005-0.05/km². The whole pre-contact circumpolar population was of order 10^5-10^6, not 10^7 for one group.
items.why_it_matters: The brief's population numbers, its 'who leads here' shares and the pressure between peoples are all density x area. A tundra culture 100x too dense, or a forager group outnumbering most farming peoples, sends the culinary pass wrong scales for surplus, trade and how a cuisine is organised. This is exactly the kind of number an amateur reader checks first.
items.recommendation: Scale density by a productivity term the world already has: NPP or the grazing / foraging / fertile goods in absolute terms, not renormalised. Let a way of life set its density per unit of productivity (forager << pastoralist < farmer). Give groups their own density defaults by way, not by people (cervid_tundra and human_forager inherit theirs). Check it against a few ethnographic bands, e.g. Binford 2001 hunter-gatherer densities.
items.verify_reason: b69f51 run.txt:498 and :504 match the finding (human_forager 107.5M at 3/km2 on 103.6 Mkm2; cervid_tundra 13.85M at 2/km2 on 10.29 Mkm2). capacity() (history.py:175-215) reads only temperature, rain, elevation and the people's preferred land, and the land multiplier is renormalised to a mean of 1 over the people's own country (spec.py:28/373), so productivity in absolute terms never enters. Counted by presence, the effective densities are ~1.0-1.35/km2. That is still 10-100x the usual forager range (~0.01-0.5/km2), and Arctic densities are lower still. PW-703 and PW-663 deal with how peoples share a cell and press on each other, not with density versus productivity, so this is a real gap. It is v2 peoples work, but the culinary scale numbers feed directly off it.

items.title: The boat 'craft ladder' gets animal sea transport backwards; its 1500 km reach was tuned to the empty-land metric
items.evidence: animal_defs.py:144-152: dogs and fowl ride canoes (since 60 kyr); sheep and goats need a planked boat (since BOATS[3] = 6 kyr, spec.py:107); horses and cattle need a 'sailing ship' (since LATE_SEA_KYR = 3 kyr, spec.py:89). On Earth, domestic goats and then cattle were taken by boat to Cyprus ~10.5-10.3 kyr ago (Vigne et al. 2011/2012, PNAS PMC3365171), sheep, goats and cattle reached Crete ~9 kyr and Britain and Ireland ~6 kyr in skin or dugout boats, and Polynesians carried pigs, dogs and chickens 2000-4000 km in canoes ~1 kyr ago. The spec.py:102 comment ties BOATS[3] = 6 kyr to 'Lapita / Polynesian voyages', but Lapita is ~3.3 kyr and remote Polynesia ~1 kyr. docs/proposals/lineages.md:511 says the planked-boat reach was raised from 800 to 1500 km because 'the empty land rose by 9 points'.
items.why_it_matters: Island and offshore peoples get no cattle or sheep for thousands of years after Earth's islanders had them, so island cuisines come out herd-poor, without dairy or dung fuel, for the wrong reason. The reach constant is a metric-chasing knob of the kind the owner rules out.
items.recommendation: Gate crossings by gap length and crew (sea share) with a modest per-animal cost, not by an animal size that needs a sailing ship. Let livestock cross short gaps (<~100-150 km) from soon after taming. Set reaches from documented crossings (Cyprus ~70-100 km at 10.5 kyr, Lapita ~850 km gaps at ~3 kyr, Polynesia ~2000-4000 km at ~1 kyr), and if the empty land changes after that, report it rather than tune for it. Fix the Lapita date in the spec.py comment.
items.verify_reason: animal_defs.py:145-152 confirms canoes carry only animals of size 0 (dog, fowl), planked boats from 6 kyr carry caprines, and cattle and horses (size 2) need a sailing ship from 3 kyr. The real-world dates are right: Vigne et al. put domestic goats and cattle on Cyprus at ~10.4 kyr, and Lapita starts ~3.3 kyr ago, so the spec.py:105 comment tying 6 kyr to 'Lapita / Polynesian voyages' is wrong. The doc (lineages.md:511) and PW-720 confirm the planked reach went 800 -> 1500 km because 800 'raised the empty land by 9 points'. That is partly mitigated: 1500 km was the old rule's value and the doc gives the remote-island voyages as the reason. The effect is limited to island herd peoples in a v2 layer, so low, not medium.

items.title: Owner belief: 'plant eaters, so mostly farmers' clashes with the ruminant body the same canon gives the fiends
items.evidence: PW-784 update (owner 2026-10-24): antelope-kin and cervid-kin 'are much more farmers than herders (plant-eater equivalents)', so seven_meals.toml sets way = 'farmer' on antelope_folk and cervid_folk. docs/proposals/culinary-dnd-intake.md:326-328 (section 4.3) gives them a rumen, 'The steppe's grass is their food directly: they need herds less than humans do' and 'grain in quantity sickens them (acidosis)'. spec.WAYS 'farmer' reads only the 'fertile' good, i.e. staple-grain cropland. run b69f51 run.txt:212: antelope-kin 'fields grow mostly sorghum and pearl millet, yams, taro and cassava, potatoes ... and rice', all high-starch staples. Real ruminants do get rumen acidosis from sudden starch loads, and they live on cellulose that humans have to farm around.
items.why_it_matters: Humans farm grain because they cannot digest grass. A grazer people with a rumen gains least from cereal farming and is harmed by its product. Unless the setting means this tension (the intake's 'they rule a bread state they cannot eat much of'), the brief gives the fiends a human grain-belt cuisine and loses their most distinctive culinary feature: eating the land directly, cud-chewing meals, hay and browse economies.
items.recommendation: Raise it with the owner as a needs-decision ticket. Option A: a herbivore way, e.g. 'grazier' or 'forage_farmer', that reads grazing and foraging with a forage-crop share (hay meadows, coppiced browse, legumes, tubers in moderation). items.title: Lactase is a fixed label from a group's birth, and it now causes dairy herds (foragers 'keep dairy herds'); the 60% fresh-milk cut-off is unsupported
items.evidence: animals.py:370: milks = max(herd, lac), commented 'a people with lactase milks, that is how it came to have it'. So human_forager (way forager, milk 0.6 at 11 kyr, seven_meals.toml) gets 'Its herders keep dairy herds of horses and sheep and goats and cattle, drinking the milk fresh' (run b69f51 run.txt:247). Foragers have no herds, and lactase persistence cannot arise without dairying. human_jangwa has milk 0.9 from 7 kyr, but in the same run takes up cattle only ~2.1 kyr ago (run.txt:263). brief.py:571 LACTASE_FRESH = 0.6: below it, milk is 'fermented, not fresh'. Real: persistence in Europe stayed rare until ~3-4 kyr ago, millennia after dairying began (Burger et al. 2020; Evershed et al. 2022 Nature 608:336). Most lactose malabsorbers tolerate about a cup of milk a day, and whether milk is fermented follows storage and climate more than the persistence share (Mongolian airag and milk tea, Maasai fresh and soured milk).
items.why_it_matters: Dairy (fresh or fermented) is one of the brief's headline culinary outputs. Getting it from a fixed label puts dairy herds on foragers. At earlier eras, persistence shows up before the herds that select for it.
items.recommendation: Make dairy depend only on herds x way of life; drop the lactase term from 'milks'. Treat lactase as a share that rises under dairying, e.g. from ~0 toward the preset value over a few kyr of a people having dairy animals. At minimum, say in the brief that it is a present-day value. Replace the 0.6 cut-off with a graded split (fresh share ~ lactase share, ferments rising with warmth and storage needs). Ask the owner whether the canon's 'margin foragers drink fresh milk' means they trade for it.
items.verify_reason: animals.py:370 milks = max(herd, lac) is real, and PW-784's fun20 update says it was meant ('a people with lactase milks too'). The result is visible in b69f51 run.txt:247: human foragers, which took up only dogs, 'keep dairy herds of horses and sheep and goats and cattle, drinking the milk fresh'. That is a clear wrong output. brief.py:571 LACTASE_FRESH = 0.6 is a hard cut-off with no source. The real-world points are correct: lactase persistence became common millennia after dairying began (Burger 2020; Evershed 2022), and malabsorbers tolerate about 12 g of lactose. The fix is small: drop lac from milks.
