items.title: Outdated domestication anchors: fowl at 8 kyr (the evidence now says ~3.5 kyr), horse at 5.5 kyr (Botai, not the ancestral line)
items.evidence: animal_defs.py TABLE: fowl anchor_kyr 8.0, tamed by {farm: 1.0, forage: 1.0}; horse anchor_kyr 5.5. Peters et al. 2022 (PNAS): unambiguous domestic chickens appear ~1650-1250 BCE (~3.5 kyr) in central Thailand, drawn in by rice and millet farming; the 8-10 kyr claims are rejected. Librado et al. 2021 (Nature 598:634): modern domestic horses (DOM2) come from the lower Volga-Don and spread across Eurasia from ~2000 BCE (~4.0-4.2 kyr). Botai horses (~3500 BCE, the 5.5 kyr date) are not their ancestors. Stored run 1df1c3 (docs/proposals/lineages.md:477): fowl tamed 7.3 kyr ago by kenku, a forager group. The human_nomad group (dnd.toml, 5 kyr) also predates mounted pastoral nomadism (~3 kyr).
items.why_it_matters: Eggs and chicken arrive ~4.5 kyr early, and with foragers as tamers. Riding and horse dairy arrive ~1.3 kyr early. Together with PW-794's 8 km/yr contact uptake (run.txt:263: savanna cattle people riding across 72% of their land), the world is over-horsed and over-fowled at earlier eras.
items.recommendation: Set fowl to ~3.5 kyr with tamers = farmers (farm share only, ideally where a grain crop is known) and horse to ~4.2-4.5 kyr. Move human_nomad to ~3-3.5 kyr. Cite the sources in the table comments.
items.verify_reason: The table gives fowl anchor 8.0 with tamers {farm, forage} and horse 5.5 (animal_defs.py:123/131). Peters et al. 2022 (PNAS) date unambiguous domestic chickens to ~3.5 kyr ago in rice and millet country, and Librado et al. 2021 (Nature) trace modern domestic horses (DOM2) to ~4.2 kyr, not Botai. Both are correct. With the x0.7-1.5 jitter, the fowl date is still about 2x too early. Easy data fix, low severity.

items.title: 'Iron' comes only from banded iron formations, a modern industrial ore; pre-industrial iron came from bog ore, laterite and ironstone almost everywhere
items.evidence: planet/lineages/land.py _ORES: 'iron': ('bif_fe',). planet/resources.py:594: bif_fe = craton x ramp(age, 1800, 2700 Myr) x exposed, so 'iron' districts exist only on exposed Precambrian cratons. dnd.toml and seven_meals.toml [[use]]: miner -> iron weight 0.7. mining.py ORE_GOODS treats the same layer as the iron a mining people works. Pre-industrial smelters (Iron Age Europe, Scandinavia, Russia, sub-Saharan Africa) mostly used bog iron, lateritic and sedimentary ironstones and siderite, which are available on most young landscapes too.
items.why_it_matters: The owner wants geology real enough for an amateur geologist. Pulling dwarves and miners toward Archaean BIF, and calling young-crust countries iron-poor, is the error that reader would spot. For a renaissance setting it also misplaces iron pots, griddles and tools in the culinary picture.
items.recommendation: Add pre-industrial iron sources to the iron good: bog iron (wetland plus a cool, wet climate on gley or peat soils), laterite/ironstone (the existing tropical-weathering profile in resources.py) and sedimentary ironstone (marine shale and sandstone basins). Keep BIF as a high-grade district, but not as the only source.
items.verify_reason: land.py:72 gives _ORES 'iron': ('bif_fe',), and resources.py:594 limits bif_fe to exposed cratons aged 1.8-2.7 Ga. resources.py has a laterite profile only for nickel (laterite_ni, :609), and nothing for bog iron or ironstone. Pre-industrial smelting did rely mainly on bog ore and sedimentary or lateritic ironstones. This is exactly the kind of geology error an amateur geologist would catch, and it shapes where miner peoples settle. Medium holds.

items.title: Salt trade capped at 450 km from source, with no sea routes: unsupported, and it drives 'salt-poor' verdicts
items.evidence: salt_reach.py:19 TRADE_CAP_KM = 450.0 ('salt is not traded further than this from its source'). Mined salt is carried 1.6x further (MINED_CAP); the cost-distance runs over land only (sea cells cost 0 and are skipped, line 39). brief.py:36 SALT_POOR_CUT_OFF = 0.25. PW-745 update: dwarves 27% cut off -> 'poor'. Real long-distance salt trade covered far more: Taoudenni to Timbuktu is ~650-750 km by caravan (the azalai) and then on down the Niger; Hallstatt and Wieliczka salt went across central Europe; salt moved by sea everywhere, and in a 'renaissance' era salt was a staple of long-distance commerce. PW-746's tuning brought the mean distance to salt from 1028 to 304 km on Earth.
items.why_it_matters: 'Salt is strategic' for the ruminant peoples in the canon (intake 4.3), and the brief turns the cap into rationing and curing advice ('inland it is traded in, dear and rationed', brief.py:867). An arbitrary cap with no sea route invents salt scarcity.
items.recommendation: Replace the hard cap with cost that rises with distance (price or abundance falling off with cost-km) and add sea legs for peoples with a sea share. Make the reach era-dependent if needed (short in the stone age, long by the classical era). Until then, label 'cut off' as an artefact of the v0 cap in the brief.
items.verify_reason: The cap exists (salt_reach.py:19), and only land cells take part in the walk. But it is cost-km, not km. River steps cost 0.5 and contact-zone steps 0.6, and mined salt goes 1.6x further, so real reach along rivers and trade zones is ~750-1100 km, which covers Taoudenni-Timbuktu-class routes. Any coast on a salty sea also gets boiled or solar salt (seafood salt_sea), so coastal and island peoples are not cut off. The finding is right that a hard cutoff with no sea legs is unsupported and the module calls itself a 'light first pass', but it overstates how far off the numbers are.

items.title: Interfertility tiers: 'T2, no offspring' from 1 Myr of divergence is stricter than real mammals
items.evidence: spec.py:256 TIER_KYR = (10, 1000, 40000): T1 under 1 Myr, T2 under 40 Myr. seven_meals.toml: 'bugbears split from goblins and hobgoblins ~2 Myr (T2, no offspring)'; dwarves, halflings and giants are T2 with humans at 1-3 Myr. Real mammals usually keep producing (often sterile) hybrids for ~2-4 Myr of divergence or more: horse x donkey (~4 Myr) gives mules, lion x tiger, cattle x yak or bison (fertile females), and camel x llama ('cama', ~11 Myr) by artificial insemination (Fitzpatrick 2004, Evolution 58:1865, on rates of hybrid inviability in mammals vs birds). Birds hybridise across tens of Myr.
items.why_it_matters: It is canon from the culinary repo and harmless for food, but it is stated as falling out of 'split depth', which implies biology. A reader who knows mules will notice, and it changes which mixed peoples or half-folk could plausibly exist.
items.recommendation: Tell the owner that real mammals give sterile hybrids up to ~2-5 Myr. Either relabel T2 'rare, usually sterile offspring' or keep the canon as an explicit fantasy rule in decisions.md, so it is not presented as biology.
items.verify_reason: The biology is right: horse x donkey (~4 Myr) gives sterile mules, and many mammals keep producing hybrids for several Myr of divergence. But the tiers and 'no offspring' come from the culinary-dnd canon (intake :125, :307 'there are no half-fiends'), and the depths are a setting (meta.tier_kyr, spec.py:417), so this is a configurable fantasy rule, not a claim about biology in the code. The only real issue is wording: the preset comment says tiers 'fall out of the split depths', which reads as biology. Worth one line in decisions.md.

items.title: Small body-note errors: 'birds taste no sweet' and 'birds smell poorly' are outdated generalisations
items.evidence: dnd.toml header and spec.py:157 body comment: 'birds feel no capsaicin' (correct) alongside 'felines taste no sweet, birds ...'. The avian stem body (dnd.toml, seven_meals.toml) has sweet = false and smell = 'low', inherited by kenku in dnd.toml. Hummingbirds (Baldwin et al. 2014, Science) and songbirds, about half of all bird species (Toda et al. 2021, Science), re-evolved sugar taste through the umami receptor. Many birds (petrels and other seabirds, vultures, kiwi) have a good sense of smell.
items.why_it_matters: These go straight into the culinary brief as body facts. A sweet-blind, smell-poor default makes every bird people's cuisine bland and sugar-free on the strength of a dated generalisation; aarakocra already had to be patched (PW-764).
items.recommendation: Default the avian stem to sweet = true or a share (passerine-like) and smell = 'normal'. Keep sweet = false and smell = 'low' as deliberate choices on specific lines, raptor-like or pigeon-like, with the real analogue in the comment.
items.verify_reason: The avian stem body (dnd.toml:680, with the header at :21) sets sweet=false and smell='low', with the comment 'birds: no sweet receptor... poor smell'. Birds did lose T1R2, but hummingbirds (Baldwin 2014) and songbirds (Toda 2021, about half of all bird species) re-evolved sweet taste through T1R1-T1R3. Many birds (procellariiforms, turkey vultures, kiwi) smell well. The generalisation is dated, and the fix is just a change to the default values.

items.title: On real Earth the rain model is ~40% too wet over land and has two-thirds of Earth's dry climates. The v1 bar does not measure it, and the fix is in v2
items.evidence: Latest earth_check (docs/review/base-climate/v1-finish/step2/earth_check.txt). Land rain outside Antarctica: mean 1118 mm vs GPCC 791 (+41%), median 830 vs 546. Koppen B share of land: model 20.3% vs Kottek 30.1% on the same cells (Peel 2007: 30.2%). In the confusion table only 54% of observed B land comes out as B. The 10-20N band (Sahel, India) gets 1579 mm vs 746, with B at 16% vs 61%. The largest codes: BWh 9.0/14.8 model/obs, Dwc 8.8/1.9, Cwa 12.0/3.0. I recomputed the obs shares from data/earth/L6.npz and got A 21.9, B 30.1, C 16.0, D 25.1, E 6.9. The scorecard rows from 2026-10-24 (docs/scorecard.jsonl) still read B 20.1-20.2% and land rain 1127-1128 mm. Earth world 577526 has B at 16.1% of all land. PW-305 (deserts too wet, Sahara 328 mm vs 35, Australia 837 vs 291) is 'wontdo' and was folded into PW-013/PW-015, which are both v2 (PW-015 blocked). Its E1 prototype (B 20.3 -> 21.9%, books stay closed) was never merged. The only test bar is Koppen group agreement >= 66% (tests/test_envelopes.py:97), which this passes at 71%. The generated-world envelope is dry 12-45% (test_envelopes.py:76).
items.why_it_matters: v1 promises hydrology that is 'real-enough for an amateur hydrologist'. Too-wet deserts and steppes and missing semi-arid belts are the first thing such a reader notices. For the culinary goal, aridity drives steppe pastoralism, dryland grains (millet, sorghum, barley), oasis farming, salt pans and dried or preserved food. A model that turns a third of Earth's drylands into Cw/Dw/A climates will under-produce exactly those peoples. Generated L7 worlds often land at 15-25% B (stored showcases: 6fbc2c 19.9%, 2a7385 23.1%, 3e9e7d 15.9%), so this is not only an Earth-terrain artefact.
items.recommendation: Make this explicit before the v1 tag. Either add an Earth rain and aridity line to the sign-off (for example B share within ~5 points of 30% and land P within ~20% of GPCC), or put a clear 'known v1 limitation: deserts and steppes too wet' in the README and overview. Re-open the PW-305 E1 mixed-layer prototype as a sound, modest step for v1, because it is a process statement, not a re-tune. Keep the larger PW-015 rework in v2. When judging peoples output, record each world's B share next to it.
items.verify_reason: The numbers check out. docs/review/base-climate/v1-finish/step2/earth_check.txt gives B 20.3 vs 30.1 (Kottek) and 30.2 (Peel), land P mean 1118 vs 791, median 830 vs 546, obs-B->B 54%, 10..20N 1579 vs 746 mm with B 16 vs 61. The 2026-10-24 scorecard rows read B 20.1-20.2 and land rain 1127-1128. The only Earth test is group agreement >= 66 (test_envelopes.py:97). PW-305 is wontdo and PW-013/015 are v2. The finding overstates in two ways. First, this is not an unsupported assumption: it is a known limitation the owner explicitly ruled on. PW-305's update of 2026-10-15 records option A ('keep PW-266, no temporary fixes; belongs to PW-013'), and the E1 prototype was put to the owner and not taken. Re-opening E1 therefore means re-asking a ruled question, not fixing an oversight. Second, it is less clear that the error carries over to generated worlds. PW-290 (2026-10-15) had L6 seeds at 28-34% B and L7 at 38-42%, drier than Earth, not wetter. That data is stale, and I did not verify the auditor's showcase shares (15-25%). The real gap is documentation. overview.md section 2.6's known-limits line names moisture transport and the high-latitude sea rain, but nowhere says that on Earth's terrain deserts and steppes are too wet (B 20 vs 30%). That belongs in the v1 limitations, and recording a B share per world for peoples review is cheap and sound.

items.title: Global rain is pinned to Earth's 1000 mm/yr, which hides the transport error and pushes it onto land
items.evidence: planet/climate.py:1670 sets `mean_mm=1000.0  # global mean precipitation, mm/yr (Earth ~1000)`. climate.py:2250 sets `wet = np.exp(0.03 * dT)`, and climate.py:2270 rescales the kernel's rain so its global mean equals mean_mm * wet. overview.md section 2.6 admits it: 'absolute wetness is set by that, not by the physics.' earth_check then reports 'global mean P: model 996, GPCP 983', which looks like a validation but is enforced. In the same file sea rain is about half of GPCP poleward of 50 degrees (60-70N: 373 vs 905; 50-60: 807 vs 1152), while tropical land is 1.4-2x too wet. With a fixed total, the missing storm-track sea rain has to show up somewhere else. The 3%/K scaling is also above the energy-limited ~1-3%/K that models give for global precipitation (Held & Soden 2006, J. Climate 19:5686).
items.why_it_matters: The constant is copied from Earth and props up the rain budget. It makes the global check pass by construction and moves the real error (too little moisture reaching the high-latitude oceans) onto land, which is part of why land is 41% too wet in finding 1. It also fixes a hothouse or icehouse world's total rain to an Earth-derived curve, whatever its ocean area or energy budget.
items.recommendation: For v1, label the global-P line in earth_check and the scorecard as 'enforced', not as a score. Track the land/sea split (land P vs GPCC, sea P vs GPCP by band) as the real metric. After v1 (with PW-013), replace the normalisation with an energy-limited global evaporation, or at least scale mean_mm by the ocean fraction and an energy term. Note 3%/K as an upper-end choice.
items.verify_reason: The code matches the claim: climate.py:1670 has mean_mm=1000, and climate.py:2250/2270-2271 apply wet = exp(0.03 dT) and rescale the kernel's rain to that mean. Two points are overstated. (1) overview.md section 2.6 already says plainly that absolute wetness is set by this, so nothing is hidden. Still, earth_check's 'global mean P: model 996, GPCP 983' line does read like a score when it is enforced, and relabelling it is cheap. (2) The rescale is one uniform multiplier, so it cannot move error from sea to land. The land/sea pattern error (sea rain poleward of 50 degrees about half of GPCP, tropical land too wet) comes from the kernel's transport (PW-013). The normalisation only fixes the total. Constraining global P is a standard, crude-but-sound move for a diagnostic rain kernel, and v1 is scoped to Earth-like worlds, where 1000 mm is a reasonable anchor. 3%/K sits at the upper end of the GCM range (Held & Soden 2006 give ~2%/K, range ~1-3), so it is defensible. The 'Earth-copied for alien worlds' point is a post-v1 concern: hothouse and water worlds were deferred by owner ruling PW-802.

items.title: 'global_temp_c' and 'dT' are not the planet's mean temperature: the label overstates warming by ~20% of the anomaly
items.evidence: planet/tectonics/output.py:164 sets `"global_temp_c": round(14.5 + sim.dT, 1)`. But dT is only an input to a fitted Earth profile: planet/climate.py:2179 has `eq, pole = 27.8 + 0.5 * dT ..., -10.4 + 1.5 * dT`, and the area-mean response of that profile is ~0.79 dT (land curve) or ~0.80 dT (sea curve). Measured on stored showcase worlds, labelled vs area-weighted mean of the temperature layer: 6fbc2c 18.3 vs 17.4; 2a7385 21.0 vs 19.6; 067778 15.3 vs 13.8; 6909cb 20.9 vs 19.2; a12762 19.1 vs 18.7. Earth 577526 is 14.4 vs 14.35, correct only at dT ~0. overview.md:113 states the opposite ('dT = global mean - 14.5'). Two things follow. First, co2_sensitivity '3 C per doubling, Earth's equilibrium sensitivity' acts on dT, so the realised sensitivity is ~2.4 C per doubling before the ice term. Second, the hellhole lines (docs/review/base-climate/v1-finish-8/README.md:9, :32: '+9.1 is 24 C global, against the 25 C line') and ice_criteria HOT = 8 C (tools/ice_criteria.py:49) are in dT units but described as global temperatures.
items.why_it_matters: Every 'X C global' in the sign-off write-ups, the viewer and the world meta is off by 1-2 C on warm worlds. The 'Earth's ECS' claim is not what the model does. Calibrations that cite Earth numbers in global-mean terms (PETM, Eocene, LGM -6 C) are being compared with a different quantity.
items.recommendation: Cheapest: compute global_temp_c as the area-weighted mean of the climate's temperature field (the run already has sim.temp), and rename dT in the docs to 'climate offset (profile shift)'. Sounder: rescale the profile's coefficients so the area mean moves 1:1 with dT. That changes calibration and goldens, so do it with the star/CO2 re-derivation the star-anchor audit already asks for (#1-#3), not separately. Restate the hellhole and HOT lines in whichever unit you choose.
items.verify_reason: output.py:164 sets global_temp_c = 14.5 + sim.dT. The profile at climate.py:2168 is eq 27.8 + 0.5 dT, pole -10.4 + 1.5 dT, shaped by s^2.3 (climate.py:88). Its area mean over the sphere moves by 0.5 + 1.0 x 1/3.3 = 0.80 dT, which matches the auditor's ~0.79-0.80. The stored world 6fbc2c has dT 3.77, so 0.8 x 3.77 + 14.5 = 17.5, against the auditor's measured 17.4 and the label 18.3. At dT ~0 the label is right (earth_check gives model 13.8 vs NCEP 14.0). The consequences follow. The realised CO2 sensitivity is ~2.4 C per doubling, not '3, Earth's ECS', though that is still near the IPCC range. The hellhole lines (dT 10.5/15.5) and ice_criteria HOT = 8 (tools/ice_criteria.py:49) are in profile-offset units but are described as global temperatures (v1-finish-8 README:31 '+9.1 is 24 C global'). The error is 1-3 C on warm worlds, a labelling and calibration-semantics issue rather than broken physics. Fixing the label (area-weighted mean of the temperature field) is cheap. Rescaling the profile should go with the star/CO2 re-derivation, as the auditor suggests.

items.title: The hellhole bar ('median > 25 C or any > 30 C global') is stricter than Earth's own Phanerozoic record
items.evidence: The bar in docs/review/base-climate/v1-finish-8/README.md:9 and v1-signoff/README.md:5 is 'no hellhole at median dT > 10.5 or max > 15.5'. v1-finish-2/README.md:99 calls it '25 C median, 30 C max'. Judd et al. 2024 (Science, 'A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature', PhanDA) find that GMST spanned 11 to 36 C over the Phanerozoic and that Earth spent more time warm than cold (https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10587582; https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/a-485-million-year-history-of-earths-surface-temperature/). Scotese et al. 2021 (Earth-Sci. Rev. 215:103503) likewise have hothouse peaks around or above 30 C (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.22511 summarises the record as rarely exceeding ~33 C). Earth's history would trip the 'any > 30 C' line. Because of finding 4, the model's dT 15.5 is really about +12 C area mean (~26.5 C), so the two errors partly cancel without anyone choosing that.
items.why_it_matters: The bar decides v1 sign-off. The first L6 2 Gyr hellhole (957317, +10.5 / 15.5, v1-signoff/README.md:39-44) and the hothouse recipe 5 -> 3 (make.py:65) were judged against it. 'Neither molten hellhole nor always-icebox' is the owner's own framing, and a line that fails Earth's Triassic or Cretaceous peaks is a quietly Earth-stricter assumption.
items.recommendation: Ask the owner (needs-decision): anchor the hot line to Earth's record in real area-mean terms. For example, treat a planet as a hellhole if its median exceeds Earth's warm-mode mean (~25 C) for most of the run, or if its maximum exceeds ~36 C. Or define it by habitability, such as tropical land warmest-month temperatures that crops and herds can't take, which suits the culinary goal better. Re-score 957317 and the hothouse preset under the restated line.
items.verify_reason: The fact holds. Judd et al. 2024 (Science 385, eadk3705) give GMST 11-36 C over 485 Myr, with more time spent warm than cold, so Earth's peaks would trip a '>30 C' max line. Because of the previous finding, the model's dT 15.5 is really ~+12.4 C area mean, about 27 C, so the line is even stricter than it reads. Three things weaken the finding. (1) PhanDA sits at the warm end of the reconstructions. Scotese et al. 2021 put most hothouse peaks around 28-32 C, so a 30 C max line is borderline rather than 'wildly' Earth-stricter, and the 25 C median line is roughly Earth's warm-mode level. (2) The bar is explicitly scoped to Earth-like presets for v1 (v1-signoff README:3-5), and hothouse and molten worlds are post-v1 by owner ruling (decisions.md 2026-10-24, PW-802). A conservative bar for 'Earth-like' is a defensible design choice, not a factual error. (3) The run's end is pinned to 'now', so a median over a run that ends at the present is not the same population as the Phanerozoic median. A needs-decision note on restating the line in area-mean terms, or on habitability terms that suit the culinary goal, is reasonable, but nothing in v1 rests on a falsehood here.

items.title: The Earth-likeness tools run at L5/L6 on 2 seeds, while v1 showcases and the owner's priority are L7. The level-dependence ticket has no milestone
items.evidence: tools/scorecard.py:57 and :32-35 run `Simulation(build_grid(6), ...)` for seeds [1, 2] and the Earth climate on data/earth/L6.npz. tools/earth_check.py:860 defaults to --level 6, though data/earth/L7.npz exists. tests/test_envelopes.py:23 runs L5 for 100-400 Myr, with run_sim's flora_end = 100 (tests/helpers.py:8), so its plant timeline is not the run's. test_earth_climate_score uses L6 (test_envelopes.py:93). PW-290 ('the same seed is ~10 points more arid at L7 than at L6', status todo, milestone null) says 'L6 checks don't carry over to the L7 showcases'. PW-741 (earth.py docstring at global_temperature) found arc outgassing making L6 ~1 C warmer than L7. The scorecard's 2-seed world block is noise: on 2026-10-24, seed 2's tree cover went 9.2 -> 26.3% and seed 1's dry share 23.1 -> 33.8% between two rows of the same day (docs/scorecard.jsonl, last 3 rows). The project's own rule is 'compare pass rates over several re-rolled draws'.
items.why_it_matters: Every Earth number cited in tickets, plus the CLAUDE.md rule 'after model changes run tools/scorecard.py', measures a coarser grid than the one users get. Rain shadows, closed basins and aridity are known to depend on cell size, so an L6 calibration can be right at L6 and wrong at L7. Two seeds can't show whether a change helped.
items.recommendation: For the v1 tag: run earth_check --level 7 once and record it next to L6. Give PW-290 a milestone, or re-measure it on current code with paired L6/L7 draws: close it if the gap has gone, otherwise call it a v1 caveat. Make the scorecard's world block either 6+ seeds or Earth-only, and say in CLAUDE.md that its 2-seed numbers are anecdotes. Optionally move the envelope fixture's flora_end to the run length (400).
items.verify_reason: tools/scorecard.py builds the Earth climate on data/earth/L6.npz with build_grid(6) and runs world scores with Simulation(build_grid(6), seed, ...). earth_check defaults to level 6 (its usage line reads '--level 6'). PW-290 is status todo with milestone null. It reports L7 ~10 points more arid than L6 for the same seed, and its data dates from 2026-10-15, before many climate changes. That conflicts with the owner's L7-over-L6 priority. One caveat: PW-290's direction (L7 drier) means the Earth-terrain over-wetting in finding 1 may partly cancel on L7 worlds. That is one more reason to re-measure L6 and L7 as pairs before the tag rather than assume either way. I did not re-verify the world-block noise between same-day rows, but a 2-seed block being anecdotal is consistent with the project's own re-rolled-draws rule.

items.title: Culinary-layer thresholds are in grid cells, so fisheries, salt routes, predator-free islands and people's reach change with grid level
items.evidence: planet/lineages/seafood.py:54 has `RUN_FLOW = 3.0  # flow (cells of runoff)` (salmon-like runs), :55 `RUN_LOSS = 0.96` per cell upstream, :46 `LICK_FLOW = 2.0`, and :59 `LAKE_CELLS = (1.0, 6.0)` (lake fishery size). planet/lineages/salt_reach.py:20 has `RIVER_FLOW = 2.0`. planet/coastform.py:93 has `ISLAND_CELLS = 3  # a landmass this small (cells) is an island free of land predators`. planet/lineages/compose.py:22 has `REACH_CELLS = 10 ... ~560 km at L7`. Per README.md:425, flow is cells x m/yr, so at 1 m/yr runoff RUN_FLOW = 3 means ~300 m3/s at L7 (3,110 km2 cells) and ~1,180 m3/s at L6 (12,450 km2). A 'poor' lake fishery is >= 1 cell (3,100 km2 at L7, 12,400 at L6). A predator-free island is <= ~9,300 km2 at L7 and ~37,000 km2 at L6. Other code in the same package already uses physical units (animals.py:179 `* 1000 / h.cell_km`, landuse.py:164 area_km2). No ticket mentions this level dependence (grep of issue-tracking for cells of runoff / level-dependent in lineages-related tickets found none).
items.why_it_matters: The v1 showcase set is 4 L6 plus 4 L7 worlds (PW-202), and peoples run on either. The same geography would give an L6 people a quarter as many salmon rivers, salt routes twice as long in km, and different predator-free islands from an L7 people. These are culinary outputs (fishing, salt, herds) that the end goal depends on, and they quietly depend on resolution rather than on the world.
items.recommendation: Convert these to physical units through the grid's cell area and spacing: m3/s for river thresholds (flow x cell_area / yr), km2 for lakes and islands, km for reach, and a per-km loss rate in place of RUN_LOSS. Add one test that runs the seafood and salt layers on the same world at L6 and L7 and checks that the shares agree within a tolerance. The work is mechanical (Haiku or Sonnet tier).
items.verify_reason: All the cited thresholds are in cell units: seafood.py:46 LICK_FLOW 2.0, :54 RUN_FLOW 3.0 (cells of runoff), :55 RUN_LOSS 0.96 per cell, :59 LAKE_CELLS (1, 6); salt_reach.py:20 RIVER_FLOW 2.0; coastform.py:93 ISLAND_CELLS 3; compose.py:22 REACH_CELLS 10 ('~560 km at L7'). README.md:423 defines flow as upstream runoff in cells x m/yr, so the same physical river carries 1/4 the flow value at L6 as at L7. Each threshold therefore means a river ~4x larger, or a lake or island ~4x larger in area, at L6. Siblings in the same package already convert through cell_km and area_km2. I found no ticket on lineages level dependence. It is a quiet resolution artefact in culinary outputs, and a mechanical fix.
